text:
Doctor: Karibu. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, I am here for my review. It has been two years since I finished my chemotherapy at the hospital in the city, and they told me I must keep checking here at the local clinic to make sure everything is okay.
Doctor: That is good to hear. You are doing very well. Do you have any new lumps, pain in your bones, or changes in your appetite?
Patient: No, doctor. I feel strong. I am eating well and working in my garden every day.
Doctor: That is excellent. I'll do a quick physical examination to check your lymph nodes and abdomen.
Patient: Please, I just want to be sure it hasn't come back.
Doctor: I have finished the exam; everything feels normal, no palpable nodes or masses. Your weight is stable. Since you are now two years post-treatment for your breast cancer, we will continue with your routine surveillance. I will schedule your next follow-up and ensure your mammogram is requested for next month.
Patient: Thank you, doctor. I am relieved to hear that.
Doctor: You are doing exactly what you should be. Keep coming for these follow-up checks as scheduled. I'll see you in six months for the next review.

24M, motorcycle boda rider, brought in after bike tipped over at low speed 2 hours ago. C/o severe pain and swelling, medial side of left ankle. Unable to bear weight.
O/E: Alert, vitals stable. Left ankle: significant swelling and bruising over the medial malleolus, point tenderness directly on the bone. Distal pulses (PT/DP) strong. Sensation intact.
Ix: Ankle X-ray: clear oblique fracture line visible through the medial malleolus.
Dx: Fracture of medial malleolus, left.
Plan: Above-knee backslab plaster applied. Advised non-weight bearing with crutches. Analgesia with Ibuprofen 400mg TDS and Paracetamol 1g QDS. Referred to district hospital orthopedics for follow-up and review for potential ORIF.

19M, student. c/o dry, hacking cough x 10 days, low-grade fever, headache, and malaise. No productive sputum. No SOB or chest pain.

O/E: T 37.7, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA. Appearance: well, not toxic. Chest: fine crepitations at R base, otherwise clear. No wheeze or accessory muscle use.

Ix: CXR (private lab) shows patchy interstitial infiltrates in RLL.

A: Mycoplasma pneumonia.

P: Azithromycin 500mg OD x 5/7. Paracetamol 1g TDS PRN for fever. Increase fluid intake and rest. Review in clinic if symptoms do not improve or if SOB develops.

S: 7yo male, c/o severe sore throat and fever x 2 days. Mother reports child is very irritable and refusing to swallow liquids. No cough or coryza.
O: Temp 38.9C, HR 115. Oropharynx: Bilateral tonsillar hypertrophy with prominent white exudates. Erythematous mucosa. Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Lungs: clear.
Ix: Rapid Strep Antigen Test: Positive.
A: Acute tonsillitis, Strep positive.
P: Amoxicillin 250mg/5ml suspension, 5ml TDS for 10 days. Paracetamol 120mg/5ml, 5ml TDS prn for fever. Advised hydration. R/v in 3 days if no improvement.

24M, student. C/O persistent generalized pruritus, worse at night for past 3 weeks. Reports several friends in the dorm also itching. No history of asthma or allergies. O/E: Multiple excoriated papules on interdigital web spaces of both hands, flexor surfaces of wrists, and axillae. No secondary bacterial infection noted. Imp: Classical scabies. Plan: Treat with Permethrin 5% cream. Instruct to apply from neck to toes, leave for 8-12 hours, wash off. Advise treating all household members/contacts simultaneously even if asymptomatic to prevent re-infestation. Wash all bedding and clothing in hot water and sun-dry. Return if no improvement in 7 days.

52M known chronic rheumatic heart disease, c/o worsening dyspnoea on exertion x2/12. Exam: wide pulse pressure, loud decrescendo diastolic murmur at left sternal border. Echo: valve thickened, central jet with diastolic backflow. Dx: Rheumatic aortic valve insufficiency. Start enalapril 5mg daily, refer for surgical review.

28F, presents with a small, painless, translucent bluish swelling on the inner lower lip x 3 weeks. It occasionally bursts, drains clear fluid, then reforms. No fever, no trauma history. O/E: 5mm soft, dome-shaped, fluctuant bluish lesion on the lower labial mucosa near the midline. No signs of infection, no induration, no associated lymphadenopathy. Salivary flow intact. Clinical impression: Mucocele of salivary gland. Plan: Advise pt to avoid biting/traumatizing the site. Excision biopsy indicated for definitive treatment and to rule out other pathology. Referred to dental clinic for minor surgical removal. Paracetamol PRN for discomfort.

24yo F c/o painful swelling on R side of labia x3/7. Difficulty walking/sitting. On exam: 3cm fluctuant, erythematous, tender tender mass at 4 o'clock position of introitus. No fever. Dx: Bartholin abscess. Plan: I&D under LA, local wound dressing with chlorhexidine, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid 625mg TDS x 5/7, sitz baths.

Doctor: Karibu. What brings you to the clinic today? Patient: Daktari, I am very tired. I can hardly walk to the market without feeling like my heart is racing and I am out of breath. It started a few months ago but now I cannot even lie flat at night. Doctor: Any chest pain, swelling of the legs, or coughing up blood? Patient: My ankles are swollen, yes. No chest pain, but I feel heavy in the chest. Doctor: Let me listen to your heart. Hmm. I am hearing a very irregular heartbeat and some extra sounds. Your blood pressure is 110/70. Let's get a chest X-ray and an ECG done here. Patient: Is it serious? Doctor: Your heart appears enlarged on the X-ray, and the ECG shows some electrical changes, but it doesn't clearly show why the heart is struggling. We don't have the ultrasound machine working today to see the valves or the pumping action clearly. My impression is that you have a generalized heart condition that is causing your heart to fail to pump effectively. I am starting you on Frusemide to help with the fluid in your legs and lungs, and Lisinopril for your heart. We need to watch your weight and salt intake. Come back when the ultrasound is repaired so we can see exactly what is happening inside.

Doctor: Karibu. Tell me, what brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Daktari, it’s my periods. They are very painful, especially the first two days. I have to miss work every month. And lately, it’s like my tummy is always heavy and swollen.
Doctor: How long has this been happening? Any pain during intercourse?
Patient: It’s been getting worse over the last year. Yes, the pain during sex is becoming difficult to ignore.
Doctor: Any history of pelvic infections or surgeries in the past?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Let me examine you. Your abdomen is slightly tender in the lower region, and the uterus feels a bit bulky and firm on bimanual exam. I don’t feel any clear masses in the adnexa.
Patient: Is it a tumor, Daktari?
Doctor: No, it doesn't feel like that. Based on the heavy, painful periods and the firm, enlarged uterus on exam, I suspect adenomyosis, where the lining grows into the muscle wall. We don't have an ultrasound machine working today, so we will manage symptomatically for now. I’ll prescribe Ibuprofen for the pain and recommend starting a low-dose oral contraceptive to help control the bleeding and tissue growth. If the pain doesn't settle, we'll need to look at further imaging once the scanner is fixed.

Doctor: Good morning. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, it's my breathing. I feel like my chest is tight and I'm always out of breath when I'm working.
Doctor: How long has this been bothering you?
Patient: It's been about three months now. I'm a dairy farmer, so I'm in the barn every day with the hay and the cows. I cough a lot after being in the shed, and sometimes I get these fever-like chills and aches.
Doctor: Any wheezing or history of asthma?
Patient: No, never. My chest just feels heavy and 'bubbly' when I breathe.
Doctor: Let me listen to your lungs. Right, I can hear fine crackles in the lower fields on both sides. No wheezes. Pulse is 95, oxygen saturation is 92% on room air.
Patient: Is it just a chest infection, doctor?
Doctor: Given your work with the mouldy hay, I suspect this is hypersensitivity pneumonitis, specifically farmer's lung. The organic dust from the hay is triggering a reaction in your lung tissue. We need to do a chest X-ray to confirm, but you need to avoid the barn for a few weeks and wear a proper mask if you must go back. I'll start you on a course of prednisolone and we'll monitor your lung function.

45F market vendor c/o severe pain in L heel, worse first steps in morning, x4/52. Pain eases after walking but returns after long standing. No hx of injury. Known HTN on amlodipine. No DM symptoms, random glucose 5.4. 

O/E: Walks with antalgic gait. Tenderness at medial aspect of L calcaneus. No swelling or erythema. Passive range of ankle motion full. No neurological deficit in feet. 

Imp: Plantar fasciitis, L foot.

Plan: Ibuprofen 400mg TDS x5/7, gentle calf stretches, advised to wear shoes with supportive heel cup and avoid flat flip-flops. Review if no improvement in 2 weeks for possible corticosteroid injection.

28F, c/o R flank pain, fever, and dysuria x3/7. Exam: high fever 38.6C, marked R costovertebral angle tenderness, suprapubic tenderness absent. Urine dipstick: 3+ leucocytes, 2+ nitrites. Dx: acute pyelonephritis. Plan: start Ciprofloxacin 500mg BD x14/7, paracetamol for pyrexia, oral fluids; return if no improvement in 48hrs.

S: 28M carpenter. c/o severe right thumb pain following work accident this morning; caught thumb in wood planer. Unable to move joint. No numbness/tingling.
O: Thumb MCP joint visibly deformed, abducted, swollen. Tenderness localized to MCP joint. Distal sensation intact to pinprick. Radial pulse 2+. No skin breach.
Ix: X-ray thumb: MCP dislocation, no obvious bony fracture seen.
Imp: Traumatic rupture of collateral ligament of finger at metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint.
Plan: Closed reduction performed under local anaesthetic block. MCP joint stable post-reduction. Applied thumb spica splint. Ibuprofen 400mg TDS for 5/7 for pain. Advised to keep elevated and return if neurovascular deficit or significant increase in pain. Review in 1 week for physiotherapy assessment.

24M, student. C/O persistent 'white spots' on upper back, chest, and shoulders for 3 months. No itching, no pain. Denies recent travel or similar symptoms in roommates. Noticed spots are more prominent after being out in the sun or sweating during sports. No fever or weight loss. O/E: Multiple hypopigmented macules with fine, powdery scaling noted on the upper trunk. Lesions coalesce in some areas. No signs of fungal infection on feet or groin. Impression: Pityriasis versicolor. Plan: Advised patient on hygiene and keeping skin dry. Prescribed Clotrimazole 1% cream, apply twice daily for 2 weeks. Advised that hypopigmentation may take time to resolve even after fungus is cleared. Follow up if no improvement.

Doctor: Karibu, Mama. Please, come in. What has been bothering you?
Patient: Doctor, my stomach has been burning since last week. It is here in the upper part, just under my ribs. It feels like fire, especially after I eat or if I drink tea.
Doctor: Do you have any vomiting or blood in your stool? Any history of ulcers in your family?
Patient: No blood, but I feel full very quickly, and sometimes I feel like bringing the food back up. It is very uncomfortable.
Doctor: Any history of taking painkillers like aspirin or ibuprofen for your joint pains?
Patient: Yes, I take the store-bought tablets whenever the knee pain gets bad.
Doctor: Let me examine you. Your abdomen is tender in the epigastrium, but there is no guarding or rigidity. Heart and lungs are clear. Your vital signs are stable, B.P. 120/80.
Patient: Is it serious? I am worried it is my heart.
Doctor: It doesn't seem to be your heart, Mama. Given the pain and your history of using those painkillers, your stomach lining is irritated. It is likely just inflammation of the stomach lining. We call it gastritis. I am prescribing you some Omeprazole to take daily and a bottle of magnesium trisilicate mixture to soothe the burning.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor. Should I stop the pain tablets?
Doctor: Yes, please stop those ones for now as they are damaging your stomach. If the pain doesn't settle or you notice black stools, come back immediately.
Patient: I understand. Thank you.

4yo boy, c/o poor night vision x2/12. Exam: bilateral Bitot's spots noted, central corneal haziness/dullness, no active purulence. Wt 11kg. Dx: Vitamin A deficiency c/w keratomalacia. Start Vitamin A caps (200,000 IU), dietary counseling, r/v 1/52.

Doctor: Karibu, Mzee. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, my chest is very heavy and I keep coughing, especially at night. It started about three days ago after I had a bad choking spell while eating ugali and drinking tea.
Doctor: Did you vomit during that choking?
Patient: Yes, I coughed violently and some of the food and liquid came up and went down the wrong pipe. I have been wheezing since then.
Doctor: Any fever? Any pain when you breathe?
Patient: No fever, but my chest feels tight and I am short of breath when I walk.
Doctor: Let me listen to your chest. Your breathing is quite noisy. I hear some crackles in the right lower lung field.
Patient: Is it pneumonia, Doctor?
Doctor: It is an inflammation in your lung. Because of that incident when you choked and aspirated your food and liquid into your airway, your lung is reacting to the material that was inhaled. We call this a pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomit. 
Patient: Should I take antibiotics?
Doctor: Since this is an aspiration issue rather than a standard infection, antibiotics are not our first priority. I want you to sit upright and we will give you a nebulizer treatment to open your airways. Monitor for fever over the next two days, and if you start coughing up foul-smelling phlegm, you must return immediately.

22yo G2P1, 14wks gestation. C/o persistent vomiting x 10 days, unable to tolerate even water. Reports significant weight loss and fatigue. No fever, no abdominal pain, no burning micturition. LMP confirmed by early dating scan. O/E: Patient looks weak, dry oral mucosa. BP 100/60, PR 98. Abdomen soft, fundus palpable 12 weeks size. No tenderness. Speculum exam shows clear cervical os. Urinalysis: +++ ketones, negative for nitrites/leucocytes. Malaria slide negative. Plan: Admit to ward for rehydration with IV Normal Saline. NPO initially then graded diet. Start anti-emetics: Promethazine 25mg IM stat, repeat TDS. Monitor I/Os, daily weight. Review in 24hrs.

45M, c/o severe recurrent frontal headaches x 2yrs, worsening frequency over last 3/12. Describes as throbbing, sometimes associated with photophobia and nausea. No aura, no focal weakness, no visual changes. Denies fever, wt loss or night sweats. BP 138/88, PR 76, BMI 27. O/E: Cranial nerves intact, no meningism, fundoscopy normal. Neurological exam non-focal. Investigated with RBS 5.4, RDT for Malaria negative. Impression: Chronic headache, currently not fitting classic migraine/tension criteria. Plan: Lifestyle modifications (sleep hygiene, hydration), Paracetamol 1g PRN. Ibuprofen 400mg TDS for 5 days. Monitor log of triggers and frequency. Return if develops red flags or neurological symptoms.

S: 24M student c/o pain and swelling on the left side of his chest after being hit by a blunt object during a football match this morning. Denies dyspnoea, dizziness, or loss of consciousness.
O: Alert, stable. BP 122/78, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 99%. Examination shows a tender, erythematous area on the lateral chest wall. No crepitus, lung fields clear bilaterally with equal air entry. No bruising noted.
Ix: Nil, patient cannot afford X-ray.
A: Superficial injury of unspecified body region.
P: Advised rest. Ibuprofen 400mg TDS x3/7 for pain. Return if worsening chest pain, difficulty breathing, or inability to move.

Doctor: Karibu. Tell me what is wrong.
Patient: Daktari, I have been having a running stomach for three days. It is very frequent and watery, and my stomach keeps cramping so much.
Doctor: Any blood in the stool? Any vomiting or fever?
Patient: No blood, but I have felt hot since yesterday. I have been drinking plain water and some black tea.
Doctor: Are you able to keep down small amounts of food?
Patient: Not really, I feel quite weak and nauseous.
Doctor: Let me check your vitals. Your pulse is a bit fast, and your skin turgor is slightly reduced. You are dehydrated.
Patient: Is it dangerous? I am very tired.
Doctor: You have a bacterial infection of the gut, likely from something you ate. We need to get your hydration back up. I am going to start you on ORS, zinc tablets, and a course of ciprofloxacin to clear the infection. 
Patient: Will I need a drip?
Doctor: Not yet. Take the ORS frequently in small sips. If you cannot keep fluids down or if you start passing blood, come back to the clinic immediately. Otherwise, return if you are not better in 48 hours.

35M c/o left ear blockage and decreased hearing x1/52, no pain or discharge. Otoscopy shows solid, dark, wax-like mass completely occluding the left external auditory canal; TM not visible. R ear clear. Dx impacted cerumen. Rx syringing with warm water and sodium bicarbonate drops; instructed on cleaning.

S: 34F, farmer from Mbeya, c/o generalized severe skin itching x3 months. No known allergies. Denies fevers, weight loss, or night sweats. Currently using local herbal soap but no improvement. No sick contacts. 

O: Skin dry with extensive excoriations, particularly on limbs and back. No primary lesions like vesicles or papules noted. No jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly. 

Ix: RBS 5.2, Hb 12.8, RPR non-reactive, BS negative. 

A: Chronic generalized itching. 

P: Start cetirizine 10mg nocte. Advise to stop use of herbal soap; use plain petroleum jelly or mild soap substitute. Avoid trigger foods if any. If no improvement in 2 weeks, will consider further workup for systemic causes. Review prn.

S: 42M, shopkeeper, c/o persistent cough x3/52, worse at night. Produces yellow phlegm, no blood. Denies chest pain or night sweats. No weight loss. Smoker (10 pk-yrs). No prior history of TB or inhaler use.
O: T 36.8, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air. Chest: clear to auscultation, occasional coarse rhonchi bilaterally, no crepitations. Heart sounds normal.
Ix: CXR requested to rule out TB, pending. Malaria RDT negative. RBS 5.2.
A: Bronchitis, unspecified.
P: Advised smoking cessation. Start Erythromycin 250mg QDS x 5/7 for symptomatic relief and mucolytics. Increase hydration. Return if fever develops or cough worsens. Review in 1/52 with CXR results.

42M, subsistence farmer, c/o progressive blurring of vision in the right eye x 6 months. Admits to intense itching on his shoulders and back. Denies night blindness or trauma. Lives near the riverbank.

O/E: Visual acuity 6/24 OD, 6/6 OS. External eye exam shows faint corneal opacity and small pigmentary changes. Skin on shoulders shows 'leopard skin' depigmentation and lichenification. Palpable subcutaneous nodules noted over the iliac crest.

Ix: Skin snip microscopy from iliac crest positive for microfilariae. 

Imp: Onchocerciasis of the eye.

Plan: Start ivermectin weight-based dose stat, repeat every 6 months. Advise on vector control (clearing brush around homestead). Urgent referral to eye clinic for slit-lamp evaluation of anterior chamber.

2yr M brought by mum c/o poor weight gain, lethargy, and recurrent cough x2/12. O/E: Wt 7kg (below 3rd centile), visible ribs, pedal oedema, sparse hair. No fever. Mid-upper arm circumference 11cm. Dx: Unspecified undernutrition. Plan: Referred to nutrition clinic, commence F-75 milk, start routine albendazole and multivitamin syrup.

S: 32M, manual laborer. C/o severe, throbbing pain in the anal region x 2 days. Sudden onset while lifting heavy sacks. Noted a painful, firm, bluish lump at the anal verge shortly after. No fever, no bleeding, no change in bowel habits.

O: General appearance uncomfortable, difficult to sit. Local exam reveals a 1.5cm, tense, tender, bluish, thrombosed lump at 3 o'clock position of the anal verge. No active bleeding, no mucosal prolapse. Digital rectal exam not tolerated due to severe pain.

Ix: Clinical diagnosis.

Assessment: Perianal venous thrombosis.

Plan: Warm sitz baths 3x daily. Paracetamol 1g TDS and Ibuprofen 400mg TDS for pain. Advised on high-fiber diet and hydration to avoid constipation. Will review in 48 hrs for possible excision if no improvement.

45F c/o worsening dull bone pain in legs and pelvic girdle x 6 months, difficulty rising from squat. Exam: waddling gait, significant bony tenderness. Labs: Low serum Ca 1.8 mmol/L, PO4 0.7 mmol/L, markedly elevated ALP, 25-OH Vitamin D < 10 nmol/L. Dx: Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia. Start high-dose oral ergocalciferol + calcium supps, review in 4/52.

24M, farmer from Nyeri, c/o intensely itchy bumps on R forearm x 2/52. States he was clearing brush and noticed small bites, but these have persisted and remain extremely pruritic despite using local herbal rub. Denies fever or joint pain.

O/E: Scattered 5-8mm firm, hyperpigmented erythematous papules on R forearm. Central punctum noted on two lesions. No surrounding cellulitis or tracking lymphangitis. No lymphadenopathy.

Ix: Malaria smear negative. Random glucose 5.2 mmol/L.

Imp: Persistent insect bite reaction (likely chiggers or similar local biting flies).

Plan: Clobetasol propionate cream 0.05% BD x 1/52, apply sparingly. Cetirizine 10mg nocte x 10 days. Advise long sleeves and clearing vegetation away from living areas. Review if signs of secondary infection or worsening.

S: 32M, manual laborer. Reports 3-week history of productive cough with whitish phlegm, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. No hemoptysis, no chest pain. No known HIV status, reports previous health as good. 

O: Thin-appearing male. T 37.9C, SpO2 96% on room air. RR 22. Auscultation: decreased breath sounds at the right apex, occasional crackles. No significant lymphadenopathy palpated. 

Ix: Rapid malaria test negative. Sputum GeneXpert requested (pending). CXR requested to check for opacities.

A: Chronic cough, constitutional symptoms.

P: Awaiting investigations. Educated on cough etiquette. Advised to return with results for definitive management. Given multivitamin and paracetamol for fever.

S: 34M patient presents with 2 weeks of sharp R-sided upper abdominal pain and spiking evening fevers. Describes sharp, dull aching pain radiating to the R shoulder. No diarrhea or bloody stools. Reports significant malaise and night sweats. History of alcohol intake.
O: Ill-appearing, febrile (38.4C). R upper quadrant tenderness with hepatomegaly (liver edge 4cm below costal margin). No guarding or rebound. Chest clear.
Ix: Rapid malaria test negative. Stool microscopy: cysts of Entamoeba histolytica present. Abdominal ultrasound shows a 6cm complex, hypoechoic, round mass in the right hepatic lobe. Hb 11.2.
A: Amoebic liver abscess.
P: Start Metronidazole 800mg TDS for 10 days. Paracetamol 1g TDS for fever. Counseling on hygiene. Review in 2 weeks for repeat ultrasound to assess resolution.

S: 42M, subsistence farmer, c/o progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and recent onset tachycardia over 3/12. Reports reduced dietary variety; mainly maize ugali and occasional greens. No history of cardiac illness or alcohol abuse. Denies visual changes or paresthesia.

O/E: Wt 58kg, BMI 19.5. Thin habitus. PR 108 (regular), BP 110/70. Heart sounds regular, no murmurs. Mild proximal muscle wasting. Neuro: normal power 5/5 but tires easily with repetition. Reflexes brisk.

Ix: RBS 5.2 mmol/L. Hb 11.8 g/dL (normocytic). ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes. LFTs normal. Rapid HIV negative. Molybdenum levels unavailable; clinical picture consistent with deficiency.

A: Progressive weakness and tachycardia, likely nutritional.

P: Start high-protein diet (beans, pulses). Prescribe multivitamins with trace elements. Follow up 2/52 for repeat ECG and weight monitoring. Return if palpitations worsen.

34F school teacher. c/o chronic lower abdominal discomfort, bloating, and altered bowel habits x1/12. Reports alternating between loose, non-bloody stools and periods of constipation. Symptoms correlate with high stress at work; no nocturnal diarrhoea, no weight loss, no anaemia. No history of travel or recent antibiotics.
O/E: General condition fair, not pale. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no organomegaly or masses. Bowel sounds normoactive. DRE: empty vault, normal sphincter tone.
Ix: Hb 13.1, stool microscopy negative for ova/cysts, H. pylori stool Ag negative. 
Imp: Functional bowel disorder.
Plan: Advise on high-fibre diet and fluid intake. Trial of antispasmodics (Hyoscine butylbromide) PRN. Keep a symptom diary. Review in 4/52 to monitor response.

45F, subsistence farmer from rural district. C/o chronic, progressive swelling of both lower limbs x 3 years. Noted recurrent 'feverish' episodes with red, painful skin on lower legs requiring local antibiotic creams. No history of DVT, trauma, or heart disease. Physical exam: Bilateral massive non-pitting edema of feet and lower legs with hyperkeratotic, warty skin changes (mossy appearance). Palpable pulses. No inguinal lymphadenopathy. Geography and clinical exam consistent with long-term exposure to volcanic soil and endemic filariasis region. Imp: Chronic lymphoedema, suspected lymphatic filariasis etiology. Plan: Elevate limbs, daily skin hygiene/moisturizing with petroleum jelly. Albendazole 400mg + Ivermectin 200mcg/kg stat dose. Advise on strict skin care to prevent secondary cellulitis. Follow up in 6 weeks to assess for resolution of inflammatory flares.

S: 42F presents with persistent fatigue, muscle cramps, and perioral numbness x3/52. Reports worsening constipation and weakness. No history of thyroid surgery or neck radiation. Not currently taking any medications. 

O: BP 118/76, HR 72. Chvostek sign positive. Trousseau sign present. Exam otherwise unremarkable. 

Ix: Serum electrolytes: Ca 1.6 mmol/L (low), Phosphate 1.8 mmol/L (high), Albumin 38g/L. Renal function normal. Corrected Ca consistent with hypocalcaemia. 

A: Hypocalcaemia, likely secondary to parathyroid dysfunction. 

P: Start Calcium carbonate 600mg TDS + Vitamin D3 1000IU daily. Send PTH and Magnesium levels to rule out hypomagnesaemia. Counsel on importance of adherence. Review in 1 week with results.

24F, 3/52 postpartum, presenting with 2/7 history of pain and swelling in L breast. C/o fever and chills. Breastfeeding exclusively. O/E: T 38.6C. L breast outer quadrant is erythematous, warm, and tender to palpation with a localized firm mass. No skin dimpling or nipple discharge. R breast soft, non-tender. Axillary lymph nodes not enlarged. Plan: Start Cloxacillin 500mg QDS x 7/7 and Paracetamol 1g TDS for pain/fever. Advised to continue breastfeeding on affected side despite pain and apply warm compresses. Patient educated on signs of systemic sepsis and instructed to return if redness spreads or mass persists.

S: 32F, P4, c/o continuous leakage of urine per vagina since prolonged obstructed labour 6 months ago at home. No control of urine. Patient uses rags to keep dry, causing secondary excoriation. No fever, no hematuria.
O: Pt looks distressed, odor of urine present. Speculum exam shows a 2cm communication between the posterior bladder wall and the anterior vaginal wall. Urine pooling in the posterior fornix.
Ix: Dye test: Methylene blue instilled into bladder via catheter confirms blue staining of vaginal pack.
A: Vesicovaginal fistula.
P: Referred to district hospital fistula camp for surgical repair. Advised on hygiene, frequent washing of perineal area, and barrier cream (zinc oxide) for excoriation. Provided with 5L clean water jugs for daily cleaning. Advised not to carry heavy loads.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama. How have you been feeling since we last saw you?
Patient: Daktari, it is the palpitations. My heart is beating so fast and irregular, like a chicken flapping its wings in my chest. It started suddenly three days ago.
Doctor: Do you have any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness?
Patient: No pain, but I feel very tired and lightheaded when I stand up. I have been taking my enalapril, but I ran out of the amlodipine last week.
Doctor: Let me listen to your heart. It is very irregular, fast, and I cannot identify a clear rhythm. Radial pulse is 134 beats per minute.
Patient: Is it dangerous? I am worried.
Doctor: Your ECG shows an irregular baseline with no clear P-waves and a rapid ventricular response. This is paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Your heart is out of its normal rhythm.
Patient: What do we do? Can you fix it?
Doctor: Since it started only three days ago, we need to try and control the rate first. I am starting you on digoxin to slow the heart down and I will increase your enalapril. We need to screen for thyroid issues too, so I’m ordering a TSH test at the lab, but we are cost-conscious so we will hold on the echo for now. You must stay on your blood pressure meds strictly.
Patient: I understand. I will be careful.
Doctor: Come back in three days for a repeat ECG. If you feel chest pain or faint, come to the emergency unit immediately.

24F, Para 2, c/o lower abdominal pain x1 week, dull aching character, radiating to back. Reports increasing vaginal discharge with unpleasant odor. No history of missed period, not on contraception. No fever, no vomiting.

O/E: T 37.2, BP 110/70, P 88. Abdomen soft, tenderness on deep palpation in both iliac fossae. Speculum exam shows purulent cervical discharge, friable cervix. Bimanual exam reveals cervical motion tenderness. Uterus not enlarged.

Ix: Urine HCG negative. Dipstick: leucocytes +, nitrites negative. Vaginal swab for wet mount pending.

Imp: Pelvic inflammatory disease.

Plan: Doxycycline 100mg BD x 14/7 and Metronidazole 400mg TDS x 14/7. Advise partner notification and treatment. Avoid sexual intercourse during treatment. Return if pain worsens or fever develops.

Doctor: Good morning. How can I help you today?
Patient: Doctor, I've been struggling for the past two months. I have this dry, hacking cough that just won't go away, and I feel so short of breath whenever I walk around the house.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or night sweats? I need to rule out TB given the duration.
Patient: No fever, and I've been eating okay, but the chest tightness is getting worse.
Doctor: Are you a smoker? Any history of working in factories?
Patient: No smoking. I work as a caretaker at a local bird farm on the outskirts of town. I spend all day cleaning the cages and collecting droppings. It’s very dusty in there.
Doctor: That’s interesting. Does the cough feel worse when you are at the farm?
Patient: Yes, definitely. On my days off, I feel a little better, but it feels like it’s becoming constant now.
Doctor: Let’s have a listen. Your chest sounds clear of wheezes, but there are some fine crackles at the bases of both lungs. Your O2 saturation is 92% at rest and drops to 88% after walking a few steps. 
Patient: Is it serious? I cannot afford the big scans.
Doctor: Based on your history of daily exposure to bird droppings and these specific findings, this is likely hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to your occupation. We call it 'bird fancier lung'. 
Patient: Will I need surgery?
Doctor: Not necessarily, but you must avoid the bird droppings immediately. I’m going to prescribe a course of prednisolone to reduce the inflammation in your lungs and we will monitor your breathing closely. If you continue to work in that environment without protection, the scarring will become permanent.

28yo G2P1 at 34wks c/o watery vaginal discharge x2/hrs, no contractions. Speculum exam: pooling of clear liquor, nitrazine test +ve. Vitals: BP 110/70, temp 36.7C. Dx: preterm premature rupture of membranes. Started on erythromycin and betamethasone, admit for monitoring.

S: 24M, bodaboda rider. c/o generalized body weakness, fever, and persistent headache x4 days. Denies cough, neck stiffness, or abdominal pain. No recent travel outside the region.

O/E: Alert, febrile (T 38.4C). BP 110/70, HR 96. Chest clear. No meningeal signs. No palpable organomegaly. No rashes.

Ix: Rapid diagnostic test for malaria negative. Urinalysis normal. Widal test pending.

A: Fever of unknown origin, viral etiology suspected.

P: Paracetamol 1g TDS PRN. Oral rehydration salts. Advised to increase fluid intake and rest. Return immediately if persistent vomiting, confusion, or severe abdominal pain develops. Follow up in 3 days if no improvement.

62M, known T2DM (poorly controlled), presents with painful ulcer on right heel x 3 weeks. States it started as a small blister after wearing new leather shoes. No fever, no chills. 
O/E: T 36.6, BP 138/88. Right heel shows 3cm x 2cm shallow ulcer with sloughy base and minimal surrounding erythema. No frank purulence. Pedal pulses weak but palpable. Sensory exam shows glove-and-stocking neuropathy. RBS 16.4 mmol/L.
Imp: Diabetic foot ulcer (Wagner grade 1). No signs of deep infection/osteomyelitis currently.
Plan: Daily saline dressings with povidone-iodine. Metformin dose increased; referred to diabetes educator. Advised strict off-loading of heel. To return in 7 days for review. If worsening redness, discharge or fever, come immediately for IV antibiotics.

28F, Para 3, presents with c/o vaginal itching, burning on micturition, and thick white discharge x1/52. Denies abdominal pain or fever. Patient uses local herbal wash occasionally. 

O/E: P 82, T 36.7. Speculum exam: moderate white, curd-like discharge noted in the vaginal vault. Cervix looks healthy, no contact bleeding. Adnexae non-tender on bimanual exam.

Ix: HVS (High Vaginal Swab) sent for microscopy. Rapid HIV negative (counseled). 

Imp: Vaginitis.

Plan: Advise to stop herbal wash. Clotrimazole 500mg vaginal pessary stat. Fluconazole 150mg oral tab stat. Reassure. Return if symptoms persist after 1/52.

Doctor: Karibu. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, I have been coughing for about five days now. It started with a scratchy throat, but now I am bringing up this greenish phlegm.
Doctor: Are you having any difficulty catching your breath or chest pains?
Patient: No, just the cough. It keeps me awake at night, and I feel quite weak.
Doctor: Any fever or chills at home?
Patient: I felt feverish on and off for the first two nights, but not really since then.
Doctor: Let me listen to your chest. Take a deep breath. Okay, again. I hear some coarse sounds in your airways, but your lungs sound clear otherwise, and your oxygen levels are good at ninety-eight percent.
Patient: Is it serious? I am worried it might be pneumonia.
Doctor: Your lungs sound clear of pneumonia. This is an acute bronchitis, likely following that viral bug you had. Your body just needs some time to clear the inflammation in your bronchial tubes.
Patient: What should I do for the cough?
Doctor: Drink plenty of warm water with lemon and honey. I will prescribe some paracetamol for the body aches and a simple cough linctus to help you sleep. If you start having trouble breathing, high fever, or if the cough doesn't improve after another week, please come back immediately.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.

S: 18-month-old male brought by grandmother. C/o poor walking, 'bowed legs' noted for 4/12. No fever, no cough, good appetite. Exclusively breastfed till 12/12, now on porridge. No supplements.

O: Wt 9.2kg. Irritable. Obvious bowing of distal femora and tibiae. Widening of wrists (metaphyseal cupping). Fontanelle closed. Chest shows rosary bead appearance at costochondral junctions.

Ix: POC Hb 10.2 g/dL. Clinical diagnosis based on classic skeletal deformities and dietary history.

Imp: Vitamin D deficiency rickets.

A/P: Education on balanced diet (eggs, fortified foods). Prescribed oral Vitamin D3 50,000 IU weekly x 8 weeks. Advise daily sunlight exposure. Follow-up in 2/12 to assess mobility and bone deformity progression.

Doctor: Good morning. What brings you in today?
Patient: Doctor, it is my feet. They have been itching so much, especially between the toes. It started after I spent a lot of time working in the damp areas of the shamba.
Doctor: Let me have a look. Take off your socks. Okay, I see peeling, macerated skin and some fissures between the third and fourth toes on both feet. Any pain?
Patient: No pain, just the persistent itch that gets worse when I take off my boots after a long day.
Doctor: Any rash anywhere else? Hands or groin?
Patient: No, just the feet.
Doctor: Okay, this is a classic fungal infection of the skin. It’s what we call athlete's foot. The humidity and the boots are keeping it moist, which the fungus loves.
Patient: Is it serious? My neighbor told me it might be something else.
Doctor: It is common here. I’m going to prescribe some Clotrimazole cream to apply twice daily. The most important thing is the hygiene: you must dry your feet thoroughly after washing, especially between the toes, and try to wear open sandals when you are not at work to let the skin breathe. Wash your socks in hot water and soap every day.
Patient: How long should I use the cream?
Doctor: Use it for two weeks consistently, even if the itching stops after a few days. If it doesn't improve or starts looking angry and red with pus, come back so we can check for a secondary bacterial infection. For now, it is just straightforward dermatophytosis of the foot. Anything else bothering you?
Patient: No, that is all. Thank you, Doctor.

14M c/o persistent diarrhea and failure to thrive. Pale conjunctiva, brittle nails, and skin rash noted. Hb 9.2g/dL. Stool MC&S unremarkable. Suspect malabsorption. Requesting zinc and magnesium levels in blood to rule out mineral transport issues. Plan: Zinc tabs, Mebendazole, review in 2/52.

Doctor: Hello, Mzee. I understand you've been having some trouble with your vision lately?
Patient: Yes, doctor. Since yesterday evening, my left eye has been very painful and my vision is all blurry, like looking through fog. I also have a bad headache on that side.
Doctor: Any nausea or vomiting with that pain?
Patient: Actually, yes, I vomited once this morning because the pain was so sharp.
Doctor: Let me have a look. I'm shining this torch—your pupil is mid-dilated and fixed. The eye is quite firm to the touch, like a hard marble compared to the right one.
Patient: Is it serious? I cannot see the clinic clock clearly with that eye.
Doctor: Your eye pressure is definitely too high. The angle where the fluid should drain is completely closed. This is a primary angle-closure attack. We need to lower this pressure immediately before you lose vision.
Patient: Can I just get some drops?
Doctor: We need to start IV acetazolamide right away and use pilocarpine drops to pull the iris open. I'll need to monitor your pressure every hour until it drops. Once it's stable, you will need a laser procedure to create a new drainage hole to prevent this from happening again.
Patient: Okay, doctor. Please do what is needed, I am very worried.
Doctor: I understand. Nurse, please start the acetazolamide infusion and give 10mg of diazepam as well to help him relax. We will reassess in 60 minutes.

S: 68M brought in by family after 'choking' on thin uji (porridge) 2 hours ago. Followed by paroxysmal coughing, wheezing, and dyspnea. No previous history of asthma. Not a smoker. 
O: T 37.2, RR 32, SpO2 89% RA. Patient appears distressed, tachypneic. Auscultation: coarse crepitations in R lower zone, occasional rhonchi. 
Ix: Chest X-ray requested to rule out aspiration, pending. 
A: Aspiration pneumonitis post-choking incident. 
P: Oxygen 4L/min via nasal prongs. IV Ceftriaxone 1g BD started empirically. Monitor saturation. Chest physiotherapy. Admit for observation and repeat CXR in 24h. Advise on careful feeding and thickened fluids.

Doctor: Karibu, Mama. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Daktari, I have this swelling here, near my belly button. It has been there for months but lately it is very painful when I cough or lift my water jerrycans.
Doctor: Let me have a look. I see it, right at the umbilicus. Does it go back in when you lie down?
Patient: Yes, it usually disappears when I am resting in bed, but pops out again as soon as I stand.
Doctor: Any nausea, vomiting, or has the color changed to red or purple?
Patient: No vomiting, but it feels very tight. I try to push it back myself sometimes.
Doctor: Any fever or history of surgery in this area?
Patient: No, no surgery.
Doctor: Okay, I have examined you. The swelling is tender but reducible. There is no sign of obstruction or strangulation, your bowel sounds are normal and you are passing stool fine. This is an umbilical hernia. Because it is causing you pain, we should discuss elective surgical repair before it gets trapped. For now, avoid lifting heavy loads and if it becomes hard, discolored, or you start vomiting, go to the emergency department immediately. I will put you on the list for the general surgeon.

42M mechanic, presented with 3-week history of numbness and tingling in the left ring and small finger. Noted weakness in grip strength. No neck pain or trauma. Symptoms aggravated by working with elbow flexed for long periods. O/E: Wasting of left hypothenar eminence and interosseous muscles. Sensory deficit over ulnar distribution of left hand. Elbow flexion test positive. Tinel's sign at the cubital tunnel positive. Power 4/5 for finger abduction. Ix: RBS normal, HIV status negative. Plan: Conservative management. Advise avoidance of prolonged elbow flexion, nocturnal splinting of left elbow in extension. Prescribed B-complex tabs and Ibuprofen 400mg TDS prn. Review in 4 weeks for reassessment of grip strength.

S: 34F presenting with 5 days of burning sensation when passing urine and frequent urge to void. Reports some lower abdominal ache but no fever or rigors. No history of STI or vaginal discharge. 
O: Vitals: BP 118/76, HR 82, Temp 36.6C. Abdomen: soft, mild suprapubic tenderness, no costovertebral angle tenderness. 
Ix: Dipstick shows 3+ blood, nitrites negative, leukocytes 3+. Microscopic examination of spun urine sample confirms presence of >50 WBCs per HPF (pyuria).
Plan: Diagnosed as acute uncomplicated UTI. Start Ciprofloxacin 500mg BD x3/7. Advise increased fluid intake. Paracetamol 1g TDS prn for pain. Review if symptoms persist beyond 48 hours.

S: 24M presenting with intense, crawling itch on his right foot for 1 week. Reports he was walking barefoot in the garden behind his hostel in Kisumu. Denies systemic symptoms like fever or cough. 
O: Vitals stable, temp 36.8C. Exam of right dorsum shows a serpiginous, erythematous, raised, pruritic track ~8cm long moving slowly towards the ankle. No secondary infection or surrounding cellulitis noted.
Ix: Clinical diagnosis made.
A: Cutaneous larva migrans (hookworm related dermatitis).
P: Advised against scratching. Prescribed albendazole 400mg daily x 3 days. Counseled on use of protective footwear when gardening. F/u if local spreading continues or secondary bacterial infection develops.

42F, presents with recurrent palpitations and dizziness. Reports feeling as if heart is 'racing out of chest' for the past 4 hours. No chest pain or syncope. Known Hx of HTN, on Amlodipine 5mg OD. O/E: Patient anxious, diaphoretic. PR 188 bpm, BP 90/60, SpO2 96%. ECG: Regular wide-complex tachycardia with RBBB morphology, AV dissociation noted on lead II rhythm strip. Ix: RBS 5.2, RFTs normal, Troponin I negative. Mx: Initial vagal manoeuvres unsuccessful. Administered Adenosine 6mg rapid IV push, followed by 12mg; sinus rhythm restored after 12mg dose. Currently stable, PR 72. Imp: Sustained VT. Plan: Admit to ward for cardiology consult and echo to rule out structural heart disease. Start amiodarone loading. Counselling on recurrence provided.

S: 12F brought by mother with chronic non-healing ulcer on right lower leg x3/12. Started as painless papule, now enlarging with undermined edges. No fever or systemic symptoms. No history of trauma. Lives near swampy area.
O: T 36.8, P 88. 4cm diameter ulcer on distal lateral calf, shallow base with yellow slough, characteristic undermined, indurated edges. No regional lymphadenopathy. Peripheral pulses palpable.
Ix: Skin swab for AFB/culture sent. Gram stain: negative for secondary bacterial infection.
A: Suspect Buruli ulcer.
P: Refer to district hospital for biopsy and confirmation. Likely needs surgical debridement and long-term rifampicin plus clarithromycin as per protocol. Advise cleaning and dressing to prevent secondary infection. Keep clean/dry. Review with surgical consult note.

48F trader, presents with 3-year history of heavy, aching legs, worsening by end of day. No history of DVT, surgery, or trauma. O/E: Visible tortuous, dilated, bluish superficial veins involving both calves and medial aspects of the thighs. No signs of venous ulceration, hyperpigmentation, or edema. Peripheral pulses (DP and PT) palpable and symmetric. BMI 29. No calf tenderness or Homan's sign. Plan: Advise on weight loss and elevation of legs while sitting in the market. Prescribe compression stockings. Refer to general surgery for review if symptoms progress to skin changes. Return PRN.

S: 18m male child brought by mother c/o delayed walking and 'bow legs' noted by family. Diet mainly porridge and breastmilk; no vitamin supplementation. No history of seizures or recent fever.

O/E: Alert but irritable. Wt 9kg (below -2SD). Physical signs: frontal bossing, prominent wrists (widening), and bilateral femoral bowing. Chest shows rachitic rosary. No muscle tetany.

Ix: RBS 4.8. Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL. Clinical suspicion for nutritional deficiency high given lack of sunlight exposure and limited diet.

Imp: Vitamin D deficiency rickets.

Plan: Stat dose Vitamin D3 100,000 IU po, follow up in 2 weeks for further supplementation. Nutritional counseling provided: diversify diet to include eggs and fortified foods. Encourage supervised morning sun exposure daily.

32F, c/o persistent right ear itch and muffled hearing x 2 weeks. No prior ear history. O/E: Right EAC filled with fluffy, white-grey debris mixed with black punctate dots. Unable to visualize TM due to fungal plug. Left ear unremarkable. Vitals: T 36.8, PR 78. No mastoid tenderness. Imp: Otomycosis. Plan: Clear EAC under otoscopy; instill clotrimazole 1% drops tds x 7 days. Keep ear dry, no cotton buds. Return if worsening pain or discharge.

42M farmer, c/o severe L ankle pain after twisting leg in a rutted path yesterday. Unable to bear weight. 
O/E: Swelling and bruising over L lateral malleolus. Marked tenderness directly over the bony prominence. No obvious deformity of the joint. Distal pulses palpable, sensation intact. 
Ix: X-ray requested to r/o fracture. 
Imp: Lateral malleolus tenderness suggestive of fracture. 
Plan: RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation). Above-knee backslab splint applied for stability until X-ray results available tomorrow. Ibuprofen 400mg TDS, Paracetamol 1g QDS prn pain. Advised to keep leg elevated and return for review with films.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama. What seems to be the problem today?
Patient: Doctor, it is this feeling of something coming down. Whenever I stand for long to cook or walk to the market, I feel a heavy bulge at the opening of my private parts.
Doctor: How long has this been happening? Did it start after your last delivery?
Patient: Yes, after the third born. It was okay at first, but now it feels like a ball sitting right there when I am tired.
Doctor: Does it stay out all the time, or does it go back in when you lie down?
Patient: If I rest, it goes back inside, but the moment I stand, it is there again.
Doctor: Do you have any leakage of urine when you cough or sneeze?
Patient: No, doctor, just the discomfort of the mass.
Doctor: Alright, let me examine you. I want you to cough for me while I look. Yes, I can see the anterior vaginal wall is bulging down through the introitus when you strain. There is no major descent of the womb itself, and the back wall seems stable.
Patient: Is it serious? I am worried it will fall out completely.
Doctor: It is a common condition after multiple births where the wall between your bladder and vagina has weakened and is pushing forward. It is an incomplete anterior vaginal wall prolapse. We will start you on pelvic floor exercises to strengthen those muscles, and I advise you to avoid heavy lifting or carrying big jerrycans of water for now. If it keeps coming down or gets uncomfortable, we can discuss a pessary next time.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor. I will try the exercises.

34M c/o inability to pull foreskin over glans x2/7, associated with increasing swelling and pain. PMH: hx of recurring balanitis. Exam: oedematous, retracted prepuce forming a tight constricting ring behind the coronal sulcus; glans engorged and dusky. No signs of necrosis. Dx: paraphimosis. Plan: manual reduction attempted, will require dorsal slit if unsuccessful. Refer to surgical clinic for future circumcision.

S: 45M c/o left-sided facial swelling and sharp, intermittent pain under the jaw, worsening during mealtimes. Symptoms started 4 days ago. No history of trauma. Denies fever or chills.
O: T 36.6, HR 82. Visible swelling in the left submandibular region. Tender on palpation. Examination of the oral cavity reveals decreased saliva flow from the left Wharton's duct; no pus expressed, but a small, firm, non-mobile pebble-like sensation noted near the duct opening.
Ix: Clinical diagnosis. No imaging available/affordable.
A: Sialolithiasis.
P: Encouraged hydration and sour candies to stimulate saliva flow. Ibuprofen 400mg TDS for pain and inflammation for 5 days. Advised warm compresses. Return if fever develops or swelling significantly increases.

32F c/o continuous leakage of urine per vagina since prolonged obstructed labour 4/12 ago. O/E: constant trickling of urine noticed, exam confirms small opening in anterior vaginal wall communicating with urethra. Dx: Urethrovaginal fistula. Plan: Refer to fistula camp for surgical repair, maintain hygiene, counsel on nutrition.

Doctor: Good morning, mama. Tell me what is wrong with the little one today. Patient: Doctor, she has this very sharp, barking cough since last night. She sounds like a dog, and she seems to be struggling to get enough air when she cries. Doctor: Let me listen. Open your mouth for me... I can hear that high-pitched inspiratory sound, the stridor, even while she is sitting quietly. Her chest is clear but that noise in her throat is concerning. Any fever? Patient: Yes, it was high last night, about thirty-eight point five. Doctor: Okay, she is quite restless. I am worried about the swelling around her windpipe. This is classic acute laryngotracheitis. I want to give her a dose of dexamethasone now to bring down that inflammation and keep her here for an hour to make sure she settles. Patient: Will she need antibiotics? Doctor: No, this is viral, so antibiotics won't help her. We will focus on the steroids and plenty of fluids. If she starts retracting her chest or seems to get more breathless at home, you must bring her back to the clinic immediately. Patient: Understood, thank you.

Doctor: Karibu, Mama. What's bothering you today?
Patient: Daktari, my body is really painful. I have a very bad headache, and my joints are aching so much I can hardly stand. I've been feeling feverish since yesterday morning.
Doctor: Have you had any rashes, or maybe any cough or sore throat?
Patient: No rashes, Daktari. Just the pain and fever. I feel very tired.
Doctor: Let me check your vitals. Temperature is 38.9. Pulse is 100. Any nausea or stomach pain?
Patient: I feel a bit nauseous when I try to eat, but no vomiting yet.
Doctor: I’ll do a rapid malaria test right now to be sure, even though you don't have the typical chills. Also need to check your blood count.
Patient: (Waiting) ... 
Doctor: The malaria test is negative. Your white count is a bit low, and the platelets are dropping, but not critical yet. This is looking like a viral fever that is going around the community right now. Many people are complaining of the same bone-breaking pains.
Patient: Is it serious? Should I take antibiotics?
Doctor: No, antibiotics won't work on this. You need to stay well-hydrated, drink plenty of ORS and plenty of water. Take paracetamol for the fever and pain. If you start bleeding from your gums or if the stomach pain becomes severe, come back to the clinic immediately. Otherwise, it should pass in a few days.

24M, construction worker. C/o painful right big toe x1/52. States he stubbed it and now the nail is digging into the side skin. No fever, no systemic symptoms. O/E: Right hallux lateral nail fold inflamed, red, and swollen with some purulent discharge at the nail edge. Mild granulation tissue present. Rest of foot exam unremarkable. Pulses palpable. Ix: None indicated. Imp: Ingrowing toenail, right hallux. Plan: Advice on proper nail trimming (straight across). Warm saline soaks TID. Topical gentian violet for antisepsis. Advised comfortable, open footwear. If no improvement, will refer for partial nail avulsion.

S: 28F G2P1, 36/40 gestation. Reports spontaneous leaking of fluid per vaginam since 04:00 yesterday morning (approx 30 hours). No regular contractions, no fever, no foul-smelling discharge. Fetal movements felt.

O: P 92, BP 110/70, Temp 37.1C. Abdomen: uterus 36/40, fetal heart rate 142 bpm. Sterile speculum exam: pooling of clear amniotic fluid in posterior fornix. Nitrazine test positive. Cervix: long, closed, firm.

Ix: FBC: Hb 11.2, WBC 9.8. Urine: NAD.

Imp: Premature rupture of membranes, latent phase (onset of labour > 24 hours).

Plan: Admit for observation and induction. Start prophylactic antibiotics (ampicillin + erythromycin). Monitor maternal temp and FHR 4-hourly. Prepare for induction with oxytocin if no spontaneous labour by morning.

34M c/o persistent upper abdominal discomfort x 3 months. Describes a burning sensation after meals and occasional bloating. No weight loss, no dysphagia, no vomiting, and no melena. No history of alcohol use or smoking. Reports self-medicating with local antacids with only temporary relief.

O/E: General condition fair, hydrated. Abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation. No organomegaly. Bowel sounds normal. T 36.6, BP 122/78.

Ix: Rapid H. pylori test (finger prick) negative.

A: Functional oesophageal or gastroduodenal disorders.

P: Start Omeprazole 20mg daily for 4 weeks. Advise on avoiding trigger foods (spicy/oily) and small, frequent meals. Return in 1 month for review if no improvement to consider further investigations.

Doctor: Karibu, what brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, it is this thing on my foot. It is very itchy, especially at night, and I see these weird red lines under the skin.
Doctor: Let me take a look. Oh, I see a raised, serpiginous erythematous track tracking across your lateral foot and towards the ankle. How long has this been there?
Patient: About ten days. I was working in the shamba without gumboots recently, and it started shortly after.
Doctor: Any fever, cough, or general body pain?
Patient: No, just the foot. It is driving me crazy with the itching.
Doctor: Right. This is cutaneous larva migrans. You likely picked up hookworm larvae from the soil while you were working. They are trapped in your skin layers.
Patient: Is it dangerous? Do I need an injection?
Doctor: Not dangerous, but very uncomfortable. No injection needed, but I will prescribe Albendazole 400mg. Take it once a day for three days.
Patient: Should I put anything on it?
Doctor: You can apply some Calamine lotion to help with the itching, but the dewormer is what will kill the larva. Most importantly, please wear boots whenever you are working in the fields in the future to prevent this from happening again.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor. I will get the medicine at the pharmacy downstairs.

S: 28M fisherman from around Lake Victoria. C/o intermittent abdominal pain, bloody stools, and general malaise for 3 months. No fever, no weight loss. Known to wade in lake water daily for work. No prior treatment.

O: Alert, mildly pale. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no hepatosplenomegaly. 

Ix: Stool microscopy shows terminal-spined ova consistent with S. mansoni. Hb 10.2 g/dL (POC).

A: Chronic schistosomiasis.

P: Praziquantel 40mg/kg single dose stat. Advised regarding avoiding direct contact with infested lake water where possible. Re-check stool in 3 months if symptoms persist. Health education on sanitation provided.

48M c/o confusion and poor memory x1/12. Known chronic alcoholic. Exam: global cognitive decline, bilateral symmetric distal limb paraesthesia, and impaired proprioception. Labs: Hb 10.2 g/dL, MCV 108 fL, B12 low. Dx: encephalopathy due to nutritional deficiency. Plan: IM thiamine, B12 supplement, nutritional counseling, review in 2/52.

Doctor: Good morning. What brings you in today?
Patient: Doctor, my stomach has been burning for the past two weeks. It is right here in the middle, just below my ribs.
Doctor: Does it hurt after eating or when you have an empty stomach?
Patient: It is worse after I eat, especially if I have spicy food or tea with a lot of milk.
Doctor: Have you noticed any blood in your stool or are you vomiting?
Patient: No blood, but I do feel a bit bloated and sometimes like I want to throw up.
Doctor: Any fever or unintentional weight loss?
Patient: No, just the pain. It is making it hard to work in the market.
Doctor: Okay, let me examine you. Soft abdomen, no masses, but tenderness in the epigastrium. No signs of an acute surgical belly. Given the history of burning, I suspect you have gastritis. We don't have scope facilities here today, so we will manage symptomatically. I am prescribing omeprazole 20mg daily before breakfast for four weeks and some aluminium hydroxide syrup for when the burning is acute. Avoid the spicy foods and strong tea for now. If you don't feel better after this course or if you start vomiting blood, you must return immediately.

32M, manual labourer, c/o persistent insomnia, poor appetite, and fatigue starting 2/52 ago after being laid off from his construction job. Reports constant worry about school fees and inability to support his family. Denies suicidal ideation or auditory hallucinations. No history of chronic medical illness. O/E: Patient looks tired, BMI 21.5. BP 124/82, PR 78. General physical exam unremarkable; no signs of anemia or malaria. Ix: Rapid HIV test (PITC) non-reactive. RBS 5.2. Imp: Likely psychological reaction to recent life stressor. Plan: Supportive counseling provided. Advised on sleep hygiene and stress management. Will trial Amitriptyline 25mg nocte for 2/52 to aid sleep. Follow-up in 2 weeks to monitor status; return sooner if mood worsens.

Doctor: Karibu, Mama. What brings you in today? Patient: Doctor, the pain in my stomach is just too much. It started last night, right here on the upper right side under my ribs. It is sharp and keeps shooting through to my back. Doctor: Have you been vomiting or having any fever? Patient: Yes, I vomited twice this morning. I feel very feverish and I am shaking. Doctor: Let me examine you. (Doctor palpates the abdomen) Does it hurt when I press here? Patient: Ouch, yes, that is very painful. Doctor: You have a positive Murphy's sign, and your temperature is 38.9 degrees. Given the nature of your pain and the fever, I am worried about an infection in your gallbladder. We need an ultrasound to confirm, but based on the clinical presentation, I suspect you have a stone blocking the duct leading to an acute infection. I am going to start you on IV fluids and IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole right now. We will need to monitor your vitals closely and check your labs. If this does not settle, you may need a referral for surgical consultation.

7M boy brought by mother, 1-week hx of raised, non-blanching red rash on both legs and buttocks. Associated with mild knee pain and abdominal colic. No fever, no hematuria, no bloody stools. Mother notes he recently recovered from a sore throat. O/E: Alert, active. T 37.1. Palpable purpura distributed symmetrically over lower limbs and buttocks. Abdomen soft, mild peri-umbilical tenderness, no guarding. Joints: knees not swollen, range of motion full. Ix: U/A shows 1+ blood, no protein. Hb 12.1. Platelets 280k. Plan: Monitor for GI/renal symptoms. Advise high fluid intake, paracetamol PRN for pain. Explain nature of the small vessel inflammation. Return immediately if severe abdominal pain or dark urine noted.

S: 8M brought by mother with painful scalp lump x 3/52. Initially thought to be a simple boil, but has expanded. No fever or sick contacts. Failed treatment with topical Gentian Violet.

O: 3x4cm boggy, tender, inflammatory plaque on the parietal scalp. Visible broken hair shafts (black dots) within the lesion. Multiple pustules with serous discharge. No lymphadenopathy. T 36.8.

Ix: Fungal microscopy (KOH) of skin scrapings: fungal hyphae and arthroconidia visualized.

A: Kerion due to tinea capitis.

P: Start Griseofulvin 10mg/kg daily. Warm saline soaks for crusting. Advise mother to avoid squeezing the lesion to prevent secondary bacterial infection. Return in 2/52 for review.

Doctor: Karibu, welcome. Tell me, what brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, it is my neck. It has been swelling up for months now, and it feels like there is a lump here in front.
Doctor: Any trouble with swallowing or breathing? Any heart palpitations or weight loss?
Patient: No, just the swelling. It's becoming quite visible, my family noticed it too.
Doctor: Let me feel. Yes, I can see a clear enlargement of the gland. It is diffuse and soft to the touch, not hard or nodular. Any family members with the same issue?
Patient: Yes, my sister and my mother both had these swellings. We live in the rural areas upcountry.
Doctor: Okay. I’m going to order a TSH test to check your thyroid function, though we don't have the kit for antibodies today. In this region, given your history and the diffuse nature of the goitre, it is most likely due to iodine deficiency in your diet. We will confirm the thyroid status first. For now, I advise you to start using iodized salt at home. If the TSH comes back abnormal, we will manage accordingly, but this is a classic presentation of a simple diffuse goitre from lack of iodine.

Doctor: Karibu, Mama. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Daktari, it is my private parts. For the last three days, I have had this terrible burning whenever I pass urine. It is very frequent, and I feel like I need to go even after I am done.
Doctor: Any lower tummy pain or fever? Do you see any unusual discharge?
Patient: My lower abdomen is aching a bit, but no fever that I noticed. I do not see any discharge, but the urine looks a bit cloudy.
Doctor: Let me check your vitals. Your temp is 37.2, so no fever. Let us perform a dipstick test on your urine. The test shows nitrites and leucocytes are positive, but no blood.
Patient: Is it a serious infection, Daktari?
Doctor: It looks like a localized inflammation of the bladder neck, what we call trigonitis. It is a common type of cystitis. Since you are not dehydrated and have no fever, we will treat it with a simple course of nitrofurantoin for five days.
Patient: Should I take any painkillers?
Doctor: Yes, take paracetamol if the pelvic discomfort continues. Drink plenty of water and please return if you notice any blood in your urine or if the pain persists after finishing the tablets.

Doctor: Jambo, karibu. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, I've had this chest cough for five days now. It started as a cold but now the cough is deep and keeps me awake at night.
Doctor: Any chest pain or difficulty breathing when you walk?
Patient: No pain, just some wheezing at night, and I feel very tired. No fever that I've noticed, though I feel warm sometimes.
Doctor: Are you coughing up any phlegm?
Patient: Yes, it's yellow, but not green or bloody.
Doctor: Let me listen to your chest. Take a deep breath. Okay, again. I hear some coarse sounds in the tubes but no crackles in the bases. Vitals are stable, temperature is 37.2, saturation 98% on room air.
Patient: Is it pneumonia, doctor? I'm worried because my neighbour was hospitalised last month.
Doctor: Based on your exam, your lungs are clear of pneumonia. You have an acute inflammation of the bronchial tubes. We see this often with the current change in weather. I don't need to order a chest X-ray or antibiotics today as it sounds viral.
Patient: So what do I do for the cough?
Doctor: Drink plenty of warm fluids and ginger tea. I will prescribe some Cetirizine for the irritation and a simple cough linctus. If you develop high fever or trouble breathing, come back immediately. Otherwise, rest up and it should clear on its own.

45yo male builder c/o painful red patch on R leg x3/7, spreading fast. Fever, chills, malaise. Exam: R lower leg warm, tender, erythematous plaque with ill-defined borders and edema, no fluctuation. Dx streptococcal cellulitis. Started on Amox/Clav 875/125mg BD x7/7 and elevate limb.

45M c/o productive cough with rusty sputum, sharp R-sided chest pain, and high-grade fevers x4/7. No night sweats, no weight loss. Known smoker. Pt took paracetamol at home with minimal relief.
O/E: T 38.6C, RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air. Bronchial breathing noted at the right lower zone, dull to percussion. 
Ix: Malaria mRDT negative. CXR requested, pending. WBC 15.2.
Imp: Pneumonia, likely lobar. 
A: Community-acquired pneumonia. 
P: Start Amoxicillin 500mg TDS and Azithromycin 500mg OD. Increase fluid intake. Return immediately if difficulty breathing worsens or persistent high fever. Review in 3 days.

Doctor: Karibu, what brings you in today? Patient: Doctor, I have this very painful swelling on the sole of my right foot. It started about a week ago, just as a small black dot, but now it's throbbing and I can hardly walk to the shamba. Doctor: Let me have a look. I see a small, elevated lesion here with a central black spot surrounded by a white halo. Any other spots? Patient: No, just that one. It’s very itchy sometimes. Doctor: Have you been walking barefoot near the sandy soil or the animal pens lately? Patient: Yes, I usually work in the compound without shoes. Doctor: This is typical of a sand flea infestation. The flea has burrowed into your skin to lay eggs. I’m going to need to remove it carefully with a sterile needle and clean the area. After that, we’ll apply some antibiotic ointment and you’ll need to keep it covered. You must start wearing closed shoes when working in the soil to prevent this from recurring. The treatment is just the extraction and keeping the wound clean. No need for systemic antibiotics unless you notice spreading redness or pus later.

42M farmer c/o lower back pain (LBP) radiating to the right buttock x 6/12. Worse with lifting heavy sacks of maize, improved with rest. No red flags: no saddle anaesthesia, no bowel/bladder incontinence, no leg weakness or numbness, no night pain or weight loss. O/E: Tenderness over L4-L5 lumbar paraspinal muscles. Straight leg raise negative bilaterally. Power 5/5 in all dermatomes. Knee and ankle reflexes intact. No evidence of disc herniation on clinical exam. Impression: Lumbar disc degeneration, non-prolapsed. Plan: Naproxen 500mg BD x 7/7, heat therapy, focus on lifting mechanics and core strengthening exercises. Advise to avoid prolonged bed rest. Return if develops radicular symptoms or neurological deficit.

42M, farmer, presents with 4-day history of high-grade fever, rigors, and generalized body aches. Reports mild cough but no shortness of breath. No abdominal pain, diarrhoea, or dysuria. Denies rash or neck stiffness. Malaria RDT negative x2. 

O/E: Febrile (38.9C), PR 108, BP 110/70. Chest clear to auscultation. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no organomegaly. No signs of meningism. 

Ix: Haemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, WBC 14.2 x 10^9/L, urinalysis unremarkable. Blood film for parasites negative.

Imp: Acute bacterial infection, focus unclear. 

Plan: Start Amoxicillin 500mg TDS for 5 days. Paracetamol 1g QDS for fever. Advise on high fluid intake and return immediately if confusion, persistent vomiting, or respiratory distress develops. Review in 48 hours if no improvement.

S: 62F, c/o painful mass at urethral opening x 2/12. Reports intermittent bright red spotting on underwear and stinging sensation during urination. No history of trauma or recent UTI symptoms. LMP 10 years ago. 
O: Vitals: BP 130/85, HR 78, T 36.6. Local exam: Small, 8mm fleshy, erythematous pedunculated lesion at the posterior urethral meatus. Tenders to palpation, bleeds easily on contact. Pelvic floor tone normal. 
Ix: UPT negative. Urinalysis: few RBCs, negative for nitrites/leucocytes. 
Imp: Urethral caruncle.
Plan: Counselled patient on benign nature of lesion. Prescribed topical oestrogen cream (Premarin) daily x 4/52 and hygiene advice. Review in 1/12; if persists or symptomatic, refer to minor surgery for excision/biopsy.

Doctor: Karibu. What brings you and the baby to the clinic today?
Patient: Doctor, my son is 18 months old. I am worried about his legs. They look like they are bowing outwards, and he seems to have trouble walking properly. He is also very restless at night.
Doctor: I see. How is his diet? Is he still breastfeeding, and does he eat solids?
Patient: He takes breastmilk and some porridge, but we don't have much meat or eggs in our diet lately.
Doctor: Let me examine him. He is quite small for his age. Looking at his legs, there is clear bowing of the tibiae. The wrists are also looking a bit widened and thickened. He is irritable, but his heart and lungs are clear.
Patient: Is it because he is not getting enough sunshine?
Doctor: It is likely a combination of his diet and lack of vitamin D. His physical findings—the bowed legs and widened wrists—are characteristic of rickets. I am going to prescribe high-dose vitamin D supplements and calcium syrup. I want you to make sure he gets some morning sun every day.
Patient: Will he need any surgery for the legs?
Doctor: Not for now. With the supplements and improved diet, the bones should start to strengthen. We will monitor him, but if the bowing gets worse or he develops any other bone pain, bring him back immediately.

28yo male, c/o intermittent fever, rigors, and drenching sweats x4/7. Temp 39.2C, no neck stiffness, spleen tip palpable. RDT positive for P. falciparum, blood smear showed 3% parasitemia. Dx P. falciparum malaria. Start AL (Artemether-Lumefantrine) 4 tabs bid x3/7, encourage fluids, review if no improvement in 48h.

S: 42M farmer c/o painful thick skin on both heels x 4/12. Works barefoot in fields. No diabetes history, no neuropathy, no peripheral vascular disease symptoms. OTC creams not helping.

O: Healthy male, not distressed. Local exam: bilateral hyperkeratotic plaques on the weight-bearing areas of the heels with deep cracks. No discharge, no signs of cellulitis, no tinea pedis features.

Ix: RBS 5.2 mmol/L. Clinical exam sufficient.

A: Painful thickening of heels due to environmental mechanical stress.

P: Advised to wear sturdy closed shoes, soak feet daily, and apply 10% salicylic acid ointment under occlusion at night. Follow up in 3/52.

S: 8F, brought by mother from boarding school with 2-week history of intense scalp itching. Mother reports child is unable to sleep due to nocturnal scratching. No known allergies. No other systemic symptoms.
O: Child appears well. Scalp examination reveals multiple excoriations on the occipital and parietal regions. Numerous small, grey-white nits firmly attached to hair shafts noted, specifically behind ears and at nape of neck. Inspection reveals live adult lice visible upon close inspection. No secondary bacterial infection or lymphadenopathy.
Ix: Nil.
Imp: Pediculosis capitis.
Plan: Advise parent on daily combing with fine-toothed nit comb. Apply benzyl benzoate lotion to clean, dry scalp; instruct to wash off after 12 hours and repeat treatment in 7 days. Advise washing all bedding and clothing in hot water. Notify school authorities to prevent cross-transmission among classmates.

42yo male, c/o dull aching pain in left loin x3/12. Hx of recurrent UTIs. Physical exam: positive left renal punch. US abdomen shows a large, branching density filling the renal pelvis and calyces consistent with a staghorn calculus. Normal Cr. Advised on surgical referral and dietary changes. Dx: Staghorn calculus.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama John. I heard you had an episode at the market yesterday. Can you tell me what happened? Patient: Yes, I was just buying vegetables when I suddenly lost touch with everything. My husband said I fell, my whole body was stiff, and I was shaking for a few minutes. I bit my tongue and wet myself. Doctor: That sounds very frightening. How long did it last? Did you have any warning before it started? Patient: Maybe two or three minutes. No, I felt perfectly fine before it happened. Doctor: Any history of head injuries, meningitis, or similar episodes in the past? Patient: No, never. I am healthy, just taking my BP meds. Doctor: I see. Your exam today is normal—neurological testing is intact, heart sounds are clear, and BP is 135/85. Given this is the first time this has ever occurred, and considering you have no history of chronic epilepsy, I believe this is a single, isolated seizure event. Patient: So I have epilepsy? Doctor: Not necessarily. It is often a one-time reaction to a remote trigger, but we need to be careful. I am ordering a routine blood glucose test and an RDT for malaria just to be sure there is no underlying metabolic or infectious stressor. For now, avoid driving or working near open fires until we see the results. We will monitor you; if it happens again, that would be a different situation.

Doctor: Good morning. How can I help you today?
Patient: Doctor, I have had this burning pain in my upper belly for the past three weeks. It gets worse after I take my painkillers.
Doctor: Which painkillers are you using, and for how long?
Patient: My back has been hurting from the farm work, so I have been taking high-dose ibuprofen tablets from the chemist every day for about a month.
Doctor: Any black stools or vomiting blood?
Patient: No, just the burning pain and some nausea.
Doctor: Let me press on your stomach. Any pain here? 
Patient: Yes, that is exactly where it hurts.
Doctor: Your vitals are stable, blood pressure is 120/80. Given your daily use of ibuprofen, this is clearly an ulcer caused by your medication. We need to stop the ibuprofen immediately and I am prescribing you omeprazole to heal the stomach lining. I will also give you paracetamol for your back pain instead. If you continue with the anti-inflammatories, the ulcer will not heal and could bleed.

34M c/o dry cough + chest tightness x4/7, no fever. O/E: coarse crackles mid-zones bilateral, SaO2 96% RA. CXR clear. Dx: Acute bronchitis. Rx: Salbutamol inhaler 100mcg prn + fluids, follow up if SOB persists.

S: 32M trader c/o painful anal lump noticed while bathing yesterday. Pt reports intermittent bright red blood on tissue paper after passing stool for the past week. Denies fever, discharge, or change in bowel habits. No previous history of similar swellings.

O: Pt looks well, not in acute distress. PR exam reveals a tender, bluish, tense, spherical mass at the anal verge, approximately 1cm in diameter. No active bleeding, no fever, no prolapse seen.

Ix: None required.

A: Perianal venous thrombosis.

P: Explained condition. Advice on sitz baths with warm saline 3x daily. Paracetamol 1g TDS PRN for pain. Fiber supplement (psyllium) to keep stools soft. Return if worsening pain or signs of infection.

45F, teacher. Presents with a painless lump on the left side of neck, noticed by family 3 months ago. Denies dysphagia, hoarseness, or palpitations. No heat intolerance, no weight loss. Family history negative for thyroid disease. O/E: Firm, non-tender, mobile 2cm nodule on left lobe. No lymphadenopathy. Thyroid function test (TSH, fT4) normal. Plan: Referred for neck US to confirm solitary nature and assess morphology. Advised to return with report for potential FNAC. Impression: Nontoxic single thyroid nodule. Reassured patient of likely benign nature pending imaging.

S: 62F farmer c/o bilateral knee pain worsening over the last 2 years. Describes persistent aching, particularly worse after long days in the field. States knees feel stiff in the mornings, taking ~20 mins to ease. No history of injury or trauma. No fever or recent weight loss. Occasional use of Panadol but minimal relief.
O: BMI 28. Gait is antalgic. Visible bony enlargement noted at medial joint lines bilaterally. Reduced ROM in both knees due to pain. No warmth, redness, or significant effusion. Distal pulses palpable.
Ix: Hb 12.1, ESR 22. Knee X-rays not currently affordable for patient.
A: Chronic knee pain.
P: Ibuprofen 400mg TDS PRN, start regular low-impact exercises, advise on weight reduction, return if symptoms worsen or local joint swelling increases.

28F, presents with a painful swelling on the left side of the introitus x4/7, gradually increasing in size and making walking difficult. Denies fever, chills, or vaginal discharge. No recent sexual partner changes. 

O/E: Soft, fluctuant, tender 4cm cystic mass at the 4 o'clock position of the left labia majora. No surrounding cellulitis or systemic signs of sepsis. 

Ix: Urine dipstick negative for UTI/STI indicators. 

Imp: Left Bartholin gland cyst. 

Plan: Warm sitz baths, ibuprofen 400mg TDS for pain. Scheduled for incision and drainage (I&D) tomorrow under local anesthesia. Advised on signs of infection like pus or high fever to return sooner. Informed consent for procedure obtained.

Doctor: Karibu. What brings you in today?
Patient: Daktari, it’s my head. I have had this terrible headache for weeks, and now my vision is getting blurry.
Doctor: Any fevers, or have you been vomiting?
Patient: Sometimes I vomit, especially in the morning. And last week I had a strange shaking in my right arm.
Doctor: Let me see. I’m checking your reflexes and eyes. Your pupils are sluggish, and there is papilloedema on the fundoscopy. Any history of eating undercooked pork?
Patient: Yes, we keep pigs at home and sometimes slaughter them.
Doctor: Right. Your blood pressure is 130/85, temp is normal. Given the focal seizure history, the chronic headache, and the farming history, I am worried about neurocysticercosis. The CT head shows multiple cystic lesions, some with scolex, and clear meningeal irritation signs. My impression is that you have meningitis due to cysticercosis. 
Patient: Is it like a worm in the brain?
Doctor: Exactly. We need to start you on albendazole and dexamethasone immediately to reduce the swelling, and some phenobarbital for the seizures. You need to stay in the ward for monitoring while we start the deworming, as the dying cysts can cause more inflammation. Do you have someone to help you at home?
Patient: Yes, my husband is here with me.

32M, manual laborer from coastal village, c/o persistent dry nocturnal cough and progressive dyspnoea x6/12. No fever, no night sweats. Reports migratory wheeze during rainy season.
