Known asthma-like symptoms, but Salbutamol MDI provides little relief. O/E: T 36.8, PR 82, SpO2 93% on RA. Chest: bilateral coarse crepitations, scattered rhonchi. No lymphadenopathy. Ix: Chest X-ray shows diffuse mottled infiltrates in lung bases. Blood smear: marked eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count 2800 cells/uL). Stool O&P: positive for Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae. Hb 12.4. Imp: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. Plan: Diethylcarbamazine 6mg/kg/day for 21 days. Advise re mosquito net use and environmental management. Follow-up in 4/52 to monitor symptoms and repeat CBC.

S: 34F, known history of childhood polyarthritis, presents with 3/12 history of progressive dyspnoea on exertion (NYHA II) and nocturnal cough. No chest pain or orthopnoea.
O: BP 120/78, HR 92 bpm regular. Apex beat displaced laterally. Auscultation reveals a loud S1, a mid-diastolic murmur at apex, and a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Chest clear to auscultation.
Ix: ECG shows P-mitrale. Rapid strep test negative. Echo report (portable unit) confirms thickened, tethered leaflets with significant regurgitant jet and mild restricted opening.
A: Rheumatic mitral valve insufficiency with associated mild stenosis.
P: Furosemide 40mg OD. Penicillin V 250mg prophylaxis BD long-term. Educated on secondary prophylaxis adherence. Review in 4/52.

34M c/o abdominal discomfort, nausea, and passage of white, flat, moving segments in stool x3/4. Denies fever or blood in stool. Stool O&P shows eggs resembling Taenia species, patient reports frequent consumption of raw undercooked beef at local butcher. Dx: Taenia saginata infection. Plan: Praziquantel 10mg/kg single dose, hygiene counseling, advise thorough cooking of meat.

22M farmer from rural Mbeya c/o progressive blurring of distance vision in both eyes x2/yr. Exam: BCVA 6/36 OD, 6/60 OS, no improvement with pinhole. Slit lamp: apical corneal thinning and protrusion with subtle Fleischer ring. Fundoscopy normal. Dx keratoconus. Advised on rigid gas permeable lenses; to refer for corneal topography at tertiary centre.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama. What seems to be the problem today?
Patient: Doctor, I am very worried. Look at my skin, these dark, round patches appeared suddenly yesterday.
Doctor: Where did they first start? Have you had them before?
Patient: No, it is the first time. They started on my hands and now I see them on my lips as well. They feel a bit warm.
Doctor: Any itching or blistering? Did you take any new medicine or herbal tea recently?
Patient: No blisters. I did take a tablet for my headache the day before yesterday—a generic Sulfamethoxazole that I had left over from my last infection.
Doctor: Did you have a reaction like this when you took that drug in the past?
Patient: Actually, yes, I remember a similar mark on my arm years ago, but it faded away, so I forgot about it.
Doctor: I see. Looking at these dusky, well-demarcated round erythematous lesions on your dorsum of hands and lips, this is consistent with a fixed drug eruption from the cotrimoxazole.
Patient: Is it dangerous? What should I do?
Doctor: It is an allergic reaction. You must stop taking that medication immediately and never take it again—tell any doctor you see that you have an allergy to Sulfa drugs. I will prescribe some calamine lotion for the irritation and a short course of oral antihistamines, Cetirizine 10mg once daily for five days. If you start feeling swelling in your throat or difficulty breathing, you must return to the emergency clinic immediately.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor, I understand.

24M, construction worker. Fell from scaffolding ~2m height, landed on right arm 2 hours ago. Complains of severe pain and inability to rotate forearm. 

O/E: Obvious deformity mid-right forearm. Localised tenderness over shaft, significant swelling. Distal pulses (radial) palpable, CRT <2s. Sensation intact to fingers, but active finger extension weak. 

Ix: X-ray forearm AP/LAT showing transverse mid-shaft fracture of radius with mild angulation. 

Imp: Fracture of shaft of radius. 

Plan: Above-elbow backslab splint applied for stabilization. Analgesia with paracetamol 1g and ibuprofen 400mg. Referred to orthopaedic clinic at district hospital for definitive management/ORIF assessment. Advised on danger signs: loss of pulse, numbness, or worsening deformity.

S: 65M, farmer. Presents with 4/7 history of painful, spreading red rash on L cheek. Reports fever, malaise, and mild frontal headache. No prior skin trauma or insect bites noted. 
O: T 38.5C, BP 124/82. Exam: Well-defined, shiny, erythematous, indurated plaque on L malar region, extending to periorbital area. Sharp raised borders. Local warmth and tenderness on palpation. No fluctuance or abscess. Regional lymphadenopathy present in L submandibular space.
Ix: RDT Malaria negative. Blood sugar: 5.2 mmol/L. 
Imp: Erysipelas of face.
Plan: Benzylpenicillin 1.2g IV stat, then switch to Amoxicillin 500mg TDS x10/7. Paracetamol 1g TDS for fever. Advised warm saline compresses. R/v in 48hrs to monitor extension or potential orbital involvement. Safety net for vision changes or high fever.

Doctor: Karibu, Mama. Pole for the long wait. What brings you here today?
Patient: Daktari, I have had this chest cough for five days now. It is very painful and I feel like there is a lot of phlegm stuck inside.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, or difficulty catching your breath when you are resting?
Patient: I felt hot and sweaty the first two nights, but no real shaking chills. Breathing is okay, just the cough is very irritating, especially at night.
Doctor: Are you coughing up any blood or do you have any chest pain when you take a deep breath?
Patient: No blood. The pain is just a dull ache from all the coughing.
Doctor: Let me listen to your chest. Deep breath in... okay, out. One more. I hear some coarse crackles that clear with coughing, but no wheezing. Your oxygen is 98% on room air. Your chest X-ray will be too expensive and I don't think you need it today given your clinical exam.
Patient: So it is not the TB? My neighbor had that.
Doctor: Your lungs sound clear of consolidation, so it is just an acute irritation of the airways. I am going to prescribe some amoxicillin and some cough syrup with guaifenesin to help you clear the mucus. Increase your fluids and get plenty of rest. If you start having high fever or find it hard to breathe, come back immediately.
Patient: Thank you, Daktari. I will follow the instructions.

Doctor: Karibu. What brings you in today?
Patient: Daktari, it’s my right ear. It has been leaking smelly pus for over six months now. Sometimes I feel dizzy, but the constant discharge is what bothers me most.
Doctor: Do you have any pain or fever with this?
Patient: Not really, just the dampness and the bad smell, and my hearing on that side is quite poor.
Doctor: Let me take a look. I'm using the otoscope now. I see a large defect in the pars tensa of the tympanic membrane. The mucosa inside the middle ear is quite inflamed, red, and there is significant purulent discharge. The ear canal itself is relatively clear, no obvious cholesteatoma crusts, but the perforation is quite central and fixed.
Patient: Is it going to heal? The clinic in the village told me to just keep it dry.
Doctor: It is a chronic suppurative process that has damaged the drum. Because it involves the tubotympanic area, we need to be aggressive with cleaning and antibiotic drops.
Patient: Can you fix it?
Doctor: I’m prescribing Ciprofloxacin ear drops, three drops twice a day for two weeks. You must keep the ear completely dry—no water when showering—use a cotton ball with Vaseline. We will see how the discharge responds. The inflammation is likely causing the hearing loss, but we will focus on clearing the infection first. If the drainage stops, we can talk about a specialist referral for surgery to patch the hole later.

S: 32M presents with 4y/o daughter. Father concerned as daughter is developmentally delayed and needs urgent assessment at the regional referral hospital. Father is seeking a referral letter and assistance with transport arrangements to facilitate her specialist review.

O: Father is alert, cooperative, and well-appearing. No personal health complaints reported during the encounter. Child is stable, resting comfortably. 

Ix: N/A.

A: Healthy individual accompanying a sick patient for medical consultation/referral.

P: Issued referral letter addressed to Pediatric Specialist at Mulago Hospital. Advised on logistics for specialist clinic visit. Explained to father that he does not require clinical intervention today but should continue monitoring child's status. Follow-up for routine care at local health center as needed.

Doctor: Good morning. How can I help you today? 
Patient: Good morning, Doctor. I've come for a check-up because I've been feeling generally unwell and my back has been aching quite a bit lately. 
Doctor: I see. Have you noticed any other changes, perhaps with your urination or swelling in your legs? 
Patient: Not really, though I do feel like I go to the toilet more frequently, especially at night. 
Doctor: I understand. Let me check your vitals quickly. Blood pressure is 135/85, which is slightly elevated but not concerning for today. I'd like to perform a routine dipstick test to screen your urine. 
(Pause while performing dipstick test) 
Doctor: The urine dipstick is showing 3+ protein. This is significant and needs further investigation to understand why this is happening. 
Patient: Is that serious? What does it mean? 
Doctor: It indicates that your kidneys are letting protein through into the urine, which shouldn't be happening. We need to rule out several things, including infections or chronic strain on the kidneys. 
Patient: Should I be worried about my diet or medication? 
Doctor: We will start by ordering a formal lab test for your urine to confirm these findings and check your creatinine to see how your kidneys are functioning. Please avoid taking any NSAIDs like ibuprofen for that back pain for now, as they can be hard on the kidneys. 
Patient: Understood. I will get the lab work done immediately. 
Doctor: Good. Once we have the formal lab result for the protein, we can determine the next step in our management. Come back with the results as soon as you have them.

42M presents with persistent nasal congestion, mouth breathing, and reduced sense of smell for over a year. Reports snoring loudly and frequent morning headaches. Denies fever, facial pain, or yellow discharge. O/E: Pale, boggy mucosa bilaterally. Large, smooth, pearly-grey masses noted filling both middle meati, obstructing airflow. Septum midline. Throat clear. No cervical adenopathy. Assessment: Chronic obstruction likely secondary to nasal polyposis. Plan: Start Fluticasone nasal spray 2 puffs daily, saline nasal rinses. Advised on chronic nature. Refer to ENT for possible surgical excision as conservative management likely insufficient given size of polyps.

32M, c/o watery diarrhoea x3/7, no blood. Feeling weak, dizzy on standing. Vitals: BP 90/60, HR 112, temp 36.8C. Skin turgor poor, mucous membranes dry. Assessment: clinical signs of dehydration. Plan: Start ORS/Zinc supplement, increase PO fluids, review tomorrow if no improvement.

S: 45F, teacher, c/o right inner eye swelling, pain, and constant tearing x 4 days. Noted thick yellow discharge in the mornings. No trauma or vision changes. No known allergies.
O: Right eye: medial canthal area is erythematous, tender, and indurated with mild warmth. Manual pressure over the lacrimal sac expresses frank purulent material from the punctum. Conjunctiva is injected, but no corneal involvement. VA 6/6 OU. Pupils equal/reactive.
Ix: Nil, clinical diagnosis.
Imp: Right dacryocystitis.
Plan: Warm compresses TID. Start topical chloramphenicol drops QID. Systemic cloxacillin 500mg QDS x 7/7. Advise follow-up if worsening or orbital cellulitis signs (fever, proptosis, restricted motility). Review in 1/52.

S: 32M, farmer from coastal region, presents with 3 months of chronic, dry, paroxysmal nocturnal cough and occasional wheezing. Denies fever or weight loss. No TB exposure. Reports frequent exposure to soil and wading in irrigation canals. 
O: T 36.8, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air. Chest: bilateral scattered wheezes, no focal crepitations. No significant hepatosplenomegaly. 
Ix: CXR: faint migratory infiltrates. FBC: marked peripheral eosinophilia (eosinophil count 2.4 x 10^9/L). Stool O&P: negative for ova. Filariasis antigen: negative. 
A: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia secondary to occult filarial infection.
P: Start Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 6mg/kg/day in divided doses for 3 weeks. Advise on continued use of protective footwear. Follow up in 4 weeks to monitor symptom resolution and repeat FBC.

24F c/o pruritus and thick white curd-like vaginal discharge x5/7. O/E: vulvar erythema, no offensive smell, pH 4.0. Micro: budding yeast seen on wet mount. Dx: Vulvovaginal candidosis. Plan: Clotrimazole vaginal pessary 500mg stat, advise loose cotton underwear, f/u if symptoms persist.

45F c/o generalized itchy rashes and facial swelling x1/7 after starting new course of traditional herbal tea for joint pain. P/E: generalized urticaria, no wheeze, BP 110/70, sats 98%. Dx: Acute allergic reaction, likely to herbal prep. Plan: stop herbals, stat Chlorpheniramine 4mg, Prednisolone 20mg x3/7, review if no improvement.

S: 24M student. Complaining of painful, throbbing right big toe for 1 week. Reports it started after he trimmed his nail too short. Difficulty wearing closed shoes. No fever, no discharge, no systemic symptoms. 

O: Right hallux medial nail fold erythematous, swollen, and tender. Small amount of seropurulent exudate visible at the nail sulcus. Nail plate is digging into the soft tissue. No palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Ix: Nil.

Imp: Ingrowing toenail, infected.

Plan: Warm saline soaks TDS. Start Cloxacillin 500mg QDS x 5 days. Advise on proper straight-across nail trimming technique. Review in 1 week for potential nail edge resection if no improvement with conservative management. Avoid closed shoes for now.

S: 62M presents with complaint of poor hearing in both ears for the past 6 months. States he feels like people are 'mumbling' during conversation, making work at the marketplace difficult. Denies ear pain, discharge, or history of dizziness. No known head trauma or ototoxic drug exposure.

O: Otoscopy: canals patent and clean. TMs grey, intact, mobile on pneumatic insufflation. Weber test: midline. Rinne: AC > BC bilaterally. 

Ix: Rapid RPR negative. RBS 5.4 mmol/L.

A: Reduced hearing acuity.

P: Referred to regional hospital for pure tone audiometry and ENT specialist review to rule out presbycusis vs other pathologies. Advised to avoid noisy work environments. Patient counseled on limitations of current primary care diagnostic tools.

S: 32F, reports chronic fatigue, dizziness, and palpitations. Heavy menstrual periods for 6 months, using standard sanitary pads. No history of melena, hematemesis, or worms. Diet mostly maize and beans.
O/E: Pale conjunctiva, tachycardia (PR 108), BP 110/70, R 18. No organomegaly.
Hb 7.2 g/dL. Peripheral blood film: microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Stool exam negative for ova/parasites. HIV test negative.
A: Severe anemia secondary to iron deficiency.
Plan: Ferrous sulphate 200mg TDS, Ascorbic acid 100mg daily. Advice on iron-rich diet (dagaa, green leafy vegetables). Advised to see Gynae at district hospital for menorrhagia. Return in 2 weeks for repeat Hb check.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama. What seems to be the problem today?
Patient: Doctor, it is my leg. It has been swelling for a long time, maybe six months now, and it feels very heavy and hard.
Doctor: Does it hurt much? And does the swelling go down at all in the morning?
Patient: It is not very painful, just tight and heavy. Sometimes it gets a bit better after resting, but by the evening, it is very big again.
Doctor: Let me see. I see the skin is thickened and looks quite rough, like orange peel in some spots. Are you able to walk to the market okay?
Patient: Yes, but I get tired easily because of the weight of the leg.
Doctor: Have you had any fevers or red streaks running up the leg?
Patient: No, doctor.
Doctor: I’m pressing here, it doesn't pit much. My impression is that you have filariasis causing this lymphedema. We don't have the blood tests to see the parasite at night, but in this area, it is the most likely cause for this type of swelling.
Patient: Is there a cure for this?
Doctor: We can't reverse the hardening that has already happened, but we must stop it from getting worse. I will prescribe you a course of albendazole and ivermectin. You must also wash the leg daily with soap and water and keep it elevated when sitting to prevent skin infections. If you notice any sudden redness, warmth, or high fever, you must return immediately.

Doctor: Karibu. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Daktari, it is my stomach. For the past two months, I have had this burning pain in the upper belly. It feels like a fire burning.
Doctor: Does the pain come after eating, or is it worse when you haven't eaten?
Patient: It is mostly when I am hungry. If I take some porridge, it settles for a while, but then it returns.
Doctor: Any history of taking painkillers like Brufen or Aspirin for your body aches?
Patient: Yes, I take Brufen quite often for my knee pain.
Doctor: Any vomiting, black stools, or unintentional weight loss?
Patient: No, doctor. Just the burning sensation.
Doctor: Let me examine your abdomen. Any pain when I press here? 
Patient: Yes, that is the spot.
Doctor: Your abdomen is soft, no masses felt. Given your history of frequent ibuprofen use and the pattern of pain, I am concerned about irritation or ulceration in the stomach or duodenum. Since we don't have a scope here, we will treat it as a general issue of the upper digestive tract. I am putting you on Omeprazole 20mg twice daily for two months. You must stop the Brufen immediately; use Panadol if the knee hurts. Avoid spicy foods and tea for now. If you notice any dark, tarry stools, report to the hospital immediately.

24M, teacher. Presents with 4-day hx of painful, unilateral scrotal swelling and low-grade fever. Denies dysuria, discharge, or flank pain. No hx of trauma or recent unprotected sex. Reported contact with a student diagnosed with 'mumps' last week in school.
O/E: T 38.2C, BP 110/70. General exam NAD. Scrotal exam reveals enlarged, tender, indurated right testis with associated epididymal fullness. No scrotal erythema. Pharynx clear, no parotitis noted currently but reports bilateral jaw pain last week.
Ix: Urinalysis negative for pyuria/nitrites. RDT malaria negative.
Imp: Mumps-related orchitis.
Plan: Rest, scrotal support, paracetamol 1g TDS PRN pain. Advise on risk of infertility/atrophy. Return if pain worsens or swelling spreads.

42M, c/o polydipsia, polyuria, and blurred vision x 3/12. Weight loss noted by spouse. Random RBS > 20 mmol/L. No current access to HbA1c testing. No symptoms of DKA. Dx: Uncontrolled DM – start Metformin 500mg BD, counsel on diet, review with fasting glucose in 2/52.

28M, carpenter. C/o severe pain and swelling in right thumb after a piece of heavy timber fell directly onto it at the construction site 2/24 ago. Unable to move the thumb, constant throbbing pain, no numbness noted. O/E: Right thumb significantly swollen and bruised at the base/shaft. Obvious deformity with crepitus on gentle palpation. Distal sensation intact to light touch, capillary refill <2s, radial pulse palpable. Ix: X-ray thumb: Clear oblique fracture of the proximal phalanx. Imp: Closed fracture of thumb proximal phalanx. Plan: Immobilize with thumb spica splint, analgesia with Paracetamol 1g TDS + Ibuprofen 400mg TDS, elevation. RTC 1/52 for repeat exam and assessment for cast. Advise on work safety and regular movement of fingers.

24M, construction worker. C/o progressive muscle weakness in both thighs and upper arms x 6/12. Reports increasing difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a squatting position. Denies dysphagia, ptosis, or sensory changes. No family history of similar weakness known. Social hx: no excessive alcohol, no history of tick bites or toxin exposure. O/E: Symmetrical proximal weakness (MRC 4/5) in deltoids and hip flexors. Tendon reflexes preserved. Gait waddling. Ix: RBS 5.4, RFTs normal, HIV non-reactive, LFTs normal. Imp: Progressive proximal muscle weakness, suspected myopathy. Plan: Referred to physiotherapy for mobility training. Requested serum CK, LDH, and baseline ECG. Advised against heavy lifting for now. Review in 4 weeks with results.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama John. What brings you in today?
Patient: Doctor, I am feeling very tired and my heart feels like it is running a race inside my chest. It comes and goes, especially when I am working in the shamba.
Doctor: How long have you been feeling this 'racing' sensation?
Patient: Maybe for the last three months, but these past two weeks it has been very noticeable, like a bird fluttering inside.
Doctor: Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting spells?
Patient: No pain, but I get dizzy sometimes when I stand up quickly. I just feel weak.
Doctor: Let me check your pulse. Hmm, it is very irregular and fast. Let's get an ECG done right now.
Patient: Is it serious? I cannot afford the big hospital in the city.
Doctor: Let's see the tracing first. The ECG shows no P-waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm, confirming atrial fibrillation. Your heart is not beating in a steady pattern.
Patient: Is it because of my pressure? I take my nifedipine daily.
Doctor: That is likely contributing. We need to start you on digoxin to control the rate and some aspirin for now to prevent blood clots. We don't have the fancy blood thinners here, so I need you to be very careful with the aspirin. We will monitor your pressure and I want to see you back in one week. Do you have someone to help you at home?

S: 24F, housewife from village, c/o intermittent fever, drenching night sweats, and severe frontal HA for 5/7. Reports associated fatigue and joint pains. No cough, no dysuria, no abdominal pain. Last malaria episode reported 8 months ago. 
O: T 38.6, BP 110/70, PR 98, RR 20. Alert, not pale, no jaundice, no neck stiffness. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no organomegaly. 
Ix: RDT (Malaria Ag) positive. Hb 11.2 g/dL. 
A: Uncomplicated malaria. 
P: Coartem (20/120) 4 tabs BD x3/7. Paracetamol 1g TDS PRN for fever. Advised on use of ITN and to return if unable to tolerate meds or persistent high fever.

28F c/o painful muscle cramps and tingling in hands x 3/7. Exam: Trousseau sign positive. Serum Ca 1.6 mmol/L, PO4 normal. No history of thyroid surgery. Dx: tetany due to acute calcium deficiency. Plan: stat IV 10% Calcium Gluconate, monitor, oral calcium/Vit D tabs.

42M, subsistence farmer from rural district, c/o progressive bilateral foot swelling x2yrs, skin becoming 'mossy' and verrucous. Denies TB/HIV. O/E: massive hyperkeratosis of dorsum of feet/lower legs, non-pitting edema, characteristic 'mossy' appearance. Dx: advanced stage podoconiosis (non-filarial elephantiasis). Plan: foot hygiene, compression, consistent shoe wearing; referral to regional clinic for further management.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama. What seems to be the problem today?
Patient: Doctor, it is my cycle. It has been very bad lately. I am losing so much blood, like I am flooding. I have to change my cloth every hour.
Doctor: How long has this been happening, and are you having any pain with it?
Patient: It started about four months ago. No real pain, just tired. I am very anaemic, I feel dizzy when I stand.
Doctor: Are you currently breastfeeding or using any contraception like the coil or injections?
Patient: No, I stopped the injection last year. I am not pregnant, I checked with a urine stick at the pharmacy.
Doctor: Let me examine you. Your conjunctiva is quite pale. I am checking your abdomen—no masses felt. Since you are not pregnant and there is no pain, this sounds like abnormal uterine bleeding. Given the volume, we need to rule out anaemia and hormonal shifts.
Patient: Is there anything to stop the flooding? I cannot go to the market like this.
Doctor: I will order a full blood count to check your haemoglobin levels. For now, I am prescribing tranexamic acid to help control the bleeding and iron tablets for your anaemia. If the blood count is very low, we may need a blood transfusion. Please come back in one week with the results.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.

28M, boda-boda rider, presented following a fall from his bike 2 hours ago. c/o severe pain and restricted movement of his right hand after bracing himself against the tarmac. No loss of consciousness or other injuries.

O/E: Stable, BP 120/80, HR 88. Right wrist shows diffuse swelling and significant tenderness over the radiocarpal area. Full range of motion not possible due to pain. Distal neurovascular status (radial pulse/capillary refill) intact; no sensory deficit in digits.

Ix: X-ray requested to rule out fracture.

Dx: Wrist injury, right.

Plan: Ibuprofen 400mg TDS for pain, elevation, and elastic bandage support. Advised on wrist rest. Patient referred to Radiology for imaging; follow up once results are available. Red flags explained for return if numbness or loss of pulse occurs.

48F teacher, presents with 3 months of polyuria, nocturia (x4), and unintended 6kg weight loss. Complains of blurry vision and recurrent vaginal candidiasis. No family history of DM reported. 

O/E: BMI 29, BP 145/90. Chest clear, abdomen soft. No signs of diabetic foot ulcers.

Ix: Random blood glucose (capillary) = 19.8 mmol/L. Urine dipstick: 4+ glucose, ketones negative.

Imp: New onset T2DM.

Plan: Start Metformin 500mg BD. Counseled on dietary changes (reduce ugali/sugary tea). Educated on symptoms of hyperglycaemia/hypoglycaemia. Refer to diabetic nurse for lifestyle education. Re-check fasting glucose and HbA1c in 2 weeks once patient has secured funds for labs.

24yo G3P2 at 28/40, c/o intermittent fevers, chills, and rigors x4/7. Pt looks pale, mild icterus. mRDT positive for P. falciparum. No proteinuria, BP 110/70. Plan: start Coartem 6-dose regimen, Paracetamol prn, advise FANC follow-up and iron-folate supplementation.

45M, farmer, presents with a painful bulge in the right groin noted 3 weeks ago while lifting heavy maize sacks. Reports the lump is more prominent after a long day of work and occasionally disappears when lying down. No history of vomiting, constipation, or recent fever. Denies urinary symptoms or change in bowel habits.

O/E: BP 128/82, HR 76. Abd soft, non-tender. Right groin exam reveals a 4x3cm reducible swelling superior to the pubic tubercle. Impulse on cough is positive. No overlying skin changes, bowel sounds normal. Testes are descended and normal, no palpable lymphadenopathy.

Imp: Right inguinal hernia, reducible.

Plan: Advise on elective surgical repair. Review for potential complications (pain, irreducible, or signs of bowel obstruction). Provided health education on heavy lifting and local surgical clinic referral pathway.

28M farmer, c/o dull, dragging scrotal pain x6/12, worse after long days working in the fields or standing. No acute trauma, no fever, no dysuria or urethral discharge. Denies scrotal swelling or mass change in morning.
O/E: Scrotum reveals palpable, soft, worm-like dilated vessels on the left side, disappearing when supine. Valsalva maneuver makes them more prominent. Right side NAD. Testes normal consistency, no nodules, no hydrocele.
Ix: Scrotal US (requested) to confirm. Urinalysis: normal.
Imp: Left scrotal varices (varicocele).
Plan: Advice on supportive underwear. Counsel regarding potential fertility impact. Paracetamol PRN for discomfort. Review in 3/12 if symptoms worsen.

Doctor: Karibu. Tell me what brings you in today.
Patient: Doctor, I have had this terrible cough for five days now. It started with a cold, but now I feel very hot and I have a sharp pain in my right chest when I take a deep breath.
Doctor: Do you have any difficulty breathing or is it just the pain?
Patient: It is mostly the pain, but I get very tired even when walking to the kitchen.
Doctor: Let me check your vitals. Your temperature is 38.9, pulse is 105, and your oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Let me listen to your chest.
Patient: Is it malaria? Everyone says it is malaria this time of year.
Doctor: Your malaria test is negative. When I listen to your right lung base, I hear crackles and bronchial breathing. Your chest X-ray shows a clear dense consolidation in the right lower lobe.
Patient: Is that serious? Do I need an injection?
Doctor: You have pneumonia. Because we don't have the specific culture results yet to know the exact bacteria, I am starting you on oral Amoxicillin and Paracetamol for the fever and pain. Keep well hydrated.
Patient: Should I take anything else?
Doctor: No, just rest. If you start having trouble breathing or your fever does not drop in 48 hours, come back immediately so we can consider stronger antibiotics or hospital admission.

Doctor: Karibu. What brings you in today?
Patient: Doctor, I have been having this pain in my lower stomach for weeks now. It’s an aching feeling, and lately, I noticed my urine looks like it has blood in it, especially at the end of the stream.
Doctor: I see. Any fever, or pain when you pass urine? Any history of swimming in the lake nearby?
Patient: No fever, but yes, the burning is there. I work at the fisheries near the lake, so I am in the water almost every day.
Doctor: That is very helpful information. Let me examine your abdomen.
Patient: It’s mostly uncomfortable right above the pubic bone.
Doctor: Yes, there is some suprapubic tenderness. I need to check a urine dipstick for you.
Patient: Okay, I have to go now. 
[Later, after urine dipstick result]
Doctor: The dipstick shows significant haematuria. Given your occupation and the history of terminal haematuria and suprapubic pain, this points strongly to a parasitic infection acquired from the lake water. I am going to prescribe Praziquantel to treat the schistosomes. Make sure you take the full dose as instructed. We should also try to avoid the lake water as much as possible, though I know that's hard with your work.

28F c/o vague abdominal discomfort and lethargy x4/52. Denies fever or recent travel. Exam: no organomegaly, bowel sounds normal. Stool O&P ordered to rule out parasites. Plan: wait for stool microscopy results; treat symptomatically for now.

Doctor: Karibu, Mama Juma. What brings you to the clinic today?
Patient: Daktari, I am feeling very tired all the time. Even after sleeping, I wake up feeling exhausted. Also, I feel like I am always cold, even when it is hot outside.
Doctor: How long has this been happening? Any issues with your hair or skin?
Patient: It started maybe three months ago. My skin is very dry and itchy, and my hair seems to be falling out a bit more when I wash it.
Doctor: Have you noticed any swelling in your neck or any changes in your voice?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Let me check your neck. The thyroid feels normal, no goitre. Your pulse is a bit slow at 58 beats per minute. Reflexes are a bit sluggish. BP is 110/70.
Patient: Is it because of the work? I am a teacher and it is very stressful.
Doctor: It could be, but I want to be sure. I will order a TSH test to see how your thyroid is working. Given your symptoms, I suspect your thyroid gland is not producing enough hormone.
Patient: Is it dangerous?
Doctor: It is manageable. If the test confirms it, we will start you on thyroid replacement medication to get your energy back to normal. We will start with the basic blood test today.

S: 42M, farmer from Narok. Complains of chronic fatigue, intermittent muscle weakness, and vague generalized body aches x 6 months. Admits to poor dietary variety, mostly maize-based diet. Denies polyuria or excessive thirst. No fever, no night sweats, no weight loss.

O/E: BP 118/78, Pulse 76 regular. BMI 19.5. Conjunctivae pale. Heart sounds normal. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurological exam: reduced power in proximal muscles (4/5) but intact sensation and reflexes.

Ix: RBS 4.8, Hb 10.2 (microcytic), HIV rapid test negative. Electrolytes and LFTs pending due to cost constraints at regional lab. 

Imp: Generalized fatigue/weakness, likely nutritional or metabolic origin.

Plan: Start ferrous sulfate 200mg TDS, multivitamin supplement. Advise on dietary enrichment. Review in 2 weeks with lab results.

S: 34M farmer c/o right knee pain and swelling after trip and fall in shamba 2 days ago. Limping, difficulty weight bearing. No history of clicking, locking, or giving way prior to this event. No fever, no chills.
O: Alert, distress due to pain. Right knee: obvious patellar swelling, warm to touch, limited range of motion due to pain. No obvious bony deformity or crepitus. Stable collateral ligaments. Distal pulses present.
Ix: Knee X-ray (AP/Lat): No fracture or dislocation seen. Soft tissue shadow noted.
A: Effusion of joint, unspecified.
P: Advised rest, RICE protocol. Panadol 1g TDS and Ibuprofen 400mg TDS for 5/7. Use of walking stick for support. Return if worsening pain, fever, or inability to bear weight after 1 week.

S: 22M brought by brother after a single episode of body shaking and LOC today. Lasted ~3 mins, spontaneous resolution. No prior history of seizures, head injury, or current illness. Not on any meds. Reports feeling 'dizzy' prior to event.
O: Alert and oriented, GCS 15. T 36.7, BP 120/80, PR 88, SpO2 99%. No tongue biting or urinary incontinence reported. Neuro exam gross intact: pupils reactive, no focal motor deficits, gait steady. Neck supple, no signs of meningism.
Ix: RDT Malaria negative. RBS 5.2. Empiric investigations deferred due to cost.
A: Single seizure of uncertain etiology.
P: Counseling on seizure precautions (avoid heights, water, open fires). Advised to record any recurrence. To follow up if further episodes occur for further workup.

Doctor: Good morning. How can I help you today?
Patient: Doctor, I have been having a lot of pain down there. It started about three days ago and it feels like a lump on the side of my vagina. It is getting very painful to walk and sit.
Doctor: I see. Are you having any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, just a lot of pressure and discomfort. It is making sitting down very difficult.
Doctor: Let me have a look. Please, lie back on the examination couch.
Patient: Okay, I am ready.
Doctor: I am performing the exam now. I see a tender, fluctuant, red swelling located at the four o'clock position of the introitus. There is no surrounding cellulitis and no active discharge from the area. It is clearly a blocked gland causing a small collection of fluid.
Patient: Is it an infection? Do I need surgery?
Doctor: It is a Bartholin gland cyst that has become quite swollen. It does not look like an abscess yet since there is no pus draining and no fever. 
Patient: What should I do for it?
Doctor: I will recommend sitz baths with warm water three times a day to help it drain naturally. I am also prescribing a course of antibiotics to prevent it from turning into an infection. If it does not improve or the pain gets worse, come back immediately so we can consider draining it.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor. Should I avoid work?
Doctor: Try to rest for a couple of days and avoid tight clothing. If the pain becomes unbearable, return to the clinic.

48F, petty trader. c/o chronic swelling of the left lower limb x3 years, progressive, now associated with heavy, aching sensation. Denies trauma or previous DVT. Known hypertensive on Amlodipine. O/E: Patient afebrile, BMI 28. Left leg shows significant non-pitting edema extending from the dorsum of the foot to the knee, with overlying skin thickening and hyperpigmentation (mossy changes). No venous ulcers. Right leg normal. Peripheral pulses palpable bilateral. Filarial antigen rapid test positive. Dx: Lymphoedema due to lymphatic filariasis. Plan: Patient education on leg hygiene and daily skincare to prevent secondary cellulitis. Compression bandaging initiated. Start Ivermectin 150mcg/kg stat dose and Albendazole 400mg. Review in 4 weeks to monitor limb volume reduction and reinforce self-care.

28yo M c/o gritty, hard nodular growths on hair shafts scalp x4/12. No associated pruritus or alopecia. PE: multiple firm, dark, adherent stony-hard concretions on distal hair shafts. No scalp lesions. Dx: black piedra. Advised to trim affected hair and maintain scalp hygiene; antifungal shampoo if persistent.

Doctor: Good morning, Mama. What brings you in today? Patient: Daktari, I have been feeling very weak lately, like my heart is racing or 'jumping' in my chest, especially when I carry the water buckets. Doctor: Any chest pain or swelling of your legs? Patient: No swelling, but I feel so dizzy sometimes. Doctor: Let me listen to your heart. Hmm, it is very irregular and chaotic. Let me check your radial pulse—yes, it does not match the beat at the heart. I am worried about your rhythm. Patient: Is it because I am tired? Doctor: Your heart is not beating in a steady pattern; it is quivering, which is what we call atrial fibrillation. We don't have an ECG machine in this clinic today, but based on the irregular pulse and your symptoms, I am sure of it. Patient: Will I need an operation? Doctor: No, but we must slow the heart rate and thin your blood to prevent a stroke. I am starting you on Digoxin and Aspirin for now. You must come back next week to the district hospital for a proper ECG and a thyroid test. Patient: Okay, Doctor. Will I be able to work? Doctor: You need to rest and avoid heavy lifting until we get the rate controlled. Come back if you feel chest pain or faint.

Doctor: Karibu, what brings you to the clinic today? Patient: Doctor, I have been feeling very down for months. I just don't have the energy to open my shop. My heart races a lot, and I worry constantly about everything—the school fees, the rent, my husband. Doctor: How is your sleep? Patient: Terrible. I lie awake at night with these racing thoughts, and in the morning, I just feel like staying in bed. I have no appetite either. Doctor: Any chest pain or trouble breathing when the heart races? Patient: Sometimes it feels tight, but the clinic nurse checked my BP and it was 125/80. Doctor: Okay, let's check your vitals. Weight is 62kg, pulse 88. Heart and lungs sound clear. Any history of thyroid issues or recent malaria? Patient: No, I am healthy otherwise. Doctor: It sounds like you are carrying a lot of pressure. Based on what you have told me—the persistent sadness, the loss of interest in your work, and this constant, overwhelming worry and physical tension—I think you have a mix of anxiety and low mood. It is common, but it needs attention so you can function again. Patient: What can I do? I don't want to be like this. Doctor: I am going to start you on a low dose of Amitriptyline at night to help with the sleep and the mood. We should also look at some counseling if you can manage it. I want you to come back in four weeks to see if the symptoms are lifting. Avoid heavy alcohol and try to take small walks even when you don't feel like it.

32M, c/o watery diarrhea x4/7, cramping abd pain, no blood/mucus. Vitals: T 37.4, HR 88, BP 118/76. Hydrated. Dx: acute GE. Plan: ORS sachets, zinc tab 20mg OD x10/7, advise on handwashing/clean water.

S: 28F c/o recurrent lower abdominal pain x4/12. Worse during cycles but also present intermittently. Reports no fever, no vaginal discharge, and no dysuria. LMP 2 weeks ago. Currently not sexually active. No history of STI.
O/E: T 36.6, PR 72, BP 118/76. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse suprapubic tenderness on deep palpation. No guarding or rebound. Speculum: cervix healthy, no discharge. Bimanual: mild tenderness on palpation of the left fornix, no mass felt.
Ix: UPT negative. Urine dip: neg for nitrites/leukocytes. Hb 11.8 g/dL.
Imp: Chronic pelvic pain, aetiology unclear.
Plan: Paracetamol 1g TDS prn for pain. Advised on pain diary. If no improvement, will consider pelvic ultrasound next visit to rule out structural pathology. Counselled on red flags (fever, heavy bleeding).
